human_text: Looks like a good, solid start.  We may have to move the Expo prep lesson in a bit, but the date is not set yet, so it can stand where it is.  Since I will likely have a range of skills and ages for this I do not want a Rubric per se, nor a direct grading system.  Instead I want 3 levels of accomplishment.  This will allow students to always progress to the next lesson and not be stuck if they are not able to do everything, while allowing more advanced students to add-on and enhance their game without making it busy work.  My basic concept is 3 levels.  Level 1: minimal.  Think MVP.  Implements a minimal set of features that allows the game to progress to the next lesson.  Level 2: complete.  Think internal Beta/Alpha.  it includes all the expected features but may lack polish and final art.  Bugs may still exist.  Level 3: Refined.  Think ready to publish.  Keep this in mind as we craft each lesson.  Finally, I will need several forms of output for each lesson (add a rule for this).  I will need a brief (1 page) lesson plan and outline.  I will need a teacher's script.  I will need a student handout (one for each engine).  I will also need a Teacher's checklist/prep guide with detailed setup.  Since I will have to setup so many different engines I want a solid detailed checklist so I can ensure I do not miss anything and find myself unprepared for class (eg. one engine build not working as expected).  To start that off, let's create installation instructions for each of the products listed along with a "Hello, World!" project test.

human_text: Do any of the options other than Unreal have a visual scripting option (like Blueprints)?
assistant_text:
Yes — five of the seven other engines have visual scripting, and it's more common than not among your lineup:

**Unity** has "Visual Scripting" (node-graph based, the direct successor to the old Bolt plugin), bundled in by default since 2021 — closest cousin to Blueprints in your lineup, same node-and-wire feel.

**GameMaker** has "GML Visual" (what used to be called Drag and Drop) — snap-together visual blocks that live right alongside text-based GML, and can even convert one-way to text code so students can see what their visual script "really" says.

**GDevelop** is visual scripting by default — its whole paradigm is event sheets (conditions → actions), not node graphs like Blueprints, but it's the primary way you build a game there. It also lets you drop in JavaScript when you outgrow it.

**Scratch** is visual too, of course — block-based drag-and-snap, MIT's classic style.

**001 Game Creator**'s "Script Editor" is node/flowchart-based (chained events, draggable connections) and is explicitly the primary, recommended way to script — there's a legacy text-scripting mode but the docs call it a dead end with no real advantages.

**Godot** is the one clear no — it had a VisualScript system in 3.x but Godot removed it entirely starting in 4.0, so current Godot is GDScript/C# text code only.

**TIC-80** is also a no — Lua (or a few other text languages) only, no visual option at all.

So your engine spread already covers the visual-vs-text spectrum nicely without needing Unreal to carry that torch alone: Scratch/GDevelop/001 Game Creator sit purely visual, Unity/GameMaker offer both side by side, and Godot/TIC-80 anchor the "real code" end.

I just moved the Unity screenshots into place.  However, while working through the exercise I encountered an error.  The errors are shown in images 42 and 43 and are related to older graphics cards (DirectX 10).  The fix is detailed below.  I don't really want to regenerate all the images.  If by chance you can remove the warning in the bottom of the image that would be grand, but if not, they can stay.
The error and fix itself (detailed below), I would like documented in a separate file and perhaps referenced in the other documents.
=====================================
While installing Unity 6.5 on an older laptop, in particular one with a GPU that does not properly support DirectX 11 or 12.  It is DirectX 10 hardware with partial DirectX 11 support. 
The indicator of this problem is two errors:
- GpuFence:Create() error
- Shader/Hidden Render Pipeline/Edge Adaptive Spatial Upsampling is not supported (in Blit FSR Upscaling)
There are two fixes:
Fix 1: Alter settings in Unity 6.5
- Project Settings -> Quality -> Render Pipeline Asset -> URP -> Renderer 2D (Renderer 2D Data) -> Post Processing : Disable on the existing, default, URP. 
- Project Settings -> Player -> Other Settings -> Graphics API for Windows 
  -- Remove DirectX 12 Support
  -- OpenGLCore (Deprecated) 
  -- move ahead of DirectX 11 Support. 
Fix 2: Downgrade to Unity 2023 LTS
Summary:
When to downgrade to Unity 2023.2 LTS
Yes, downgrade if:
- You want to do 3D work (even basic 3D)
- You want to use DX11 instead of deprecated OpenGL (better performance, more features)
- You want better stability on older hardware without GPU fence errors
- You're doing early 3D learning (low-poly models, simple lighting, basic shaders)
Stay on Unity 6.5 with OpenGL if:
- You're focused on 2D learning (sprites, tilemaps, 2D physics)
- Your current setup works without crashes
- You don't need advanced rendering features
- What you can still do for 3D on NVS 3100M
Even with your hardware limits, you can learn:
- Low-poly 3D modeling (simple shapes, basic meshes)
- Basic lighting (baked lightmaps, simple point/directional lights)
- Standard shaders (SM 3.0-4.0, no compute shaders)
- Simple animations (rigged characters, basic mechanics)
- Basic physics (colliders, rigidbodies)
- URP rendering (without advanced post-processing or volumetrics)
You can't do (hardware-limited):
- HDRP (requires SM 5.0+, compute shaders)
- Real-time global illumination
- Advanced particle systems (GPU-based)
- High-poly models with complex shaders
- VR/AR development
Is it usable for early 3D learning?
- Yes, absolutely. Many successful indie games started on far weaker hardware. The key is:
- Low-poly, stylized art (not photorealistic)
- Baked lighting (not real-time)
- Efficient shaders (simple, not PBR-heavy)
- Small scenes (not open-world)
Unity 2023.2 LTS with DX11 on your NVS 3100M would handle all of this fine for learning purposes. You'd be able to complete tutorials, build small 3D prototypes, and learn core concepts without hitting hard walls.
Bottom line
- For 2D learning: Stay on Unity 6.5 + OpenGL (your current setup works)
- For 3D learning: Downgrade to Unity 2023.2 LTS + DX11 (better compatibility, no GPU fence errors)
- Either way: You'll be limited by hardware, but not blocked from learning fundamentals
Your hardware is "potato" by modern standards, but it's still capable of teaching you game development basics. The real limit is what you can ship, not what you can learn.

human_text: Testing 001 Game Creator right now.  It seems its default save location is in Documents.  I can see how to change that anywhere.  How does one change the save directory?
assistant_text:
That confirms it — good source. Here's the answer:

By default, 001 Game Creator stores all games in `C:\Users\[Username]\Documents\My 001 Games\`. To change that:

On the New/Open Game window (the screen you see when you launch the app or go to File > New Game / Open Game), look for the ellipsis (`...`) button in the bottom-left corner, underneath the game thumbnail area. Click it, choose **Browse...** from the dropdown, and pick whatever folder you want new projects to live in going forward.

A couple of related notes, since you're testing this for the class:
- That same ellipsis button also lets you relocate the "Demos" and "Examples" folders if you want those elsewhere too.
- Save-game data and settings files live in separate per-project folders regardless of this setting: `Documents\001\Games\[Game]\SETTINGS.INI` for the Save Setting event, and `Documents\001\Games\[Game]\SAVE*.1SV` for the built-in save system.

If you want your 001 projects to land next to your other engines' projects (matching the `--fs` trick we set up for TIC-80's working folder), this is the same idea — just pick that folder via Browse.

Sources:
- [001 Game Creator | Getting Started](https://001gamecreator.com/wiki/getstarted/)

human_text: I have downloads of of the installers for Scratch, Godot, Unity Hub (not Unity Editor), GameMaker, GDevelop, Tic80 and the trial of 001GameCreator.  Is it possible to download everything needed for Unity and Unreal to do offline installation?  Also, I did not note (except for Unity and Unreal) if any of the other installers were similar in that they were not fully self contained.  Do any of others need internet access to install?
assistant_text:
Let me get the precise official steps for both.

**Unity: yes, fully offline install is possible.** On a computer with internet, run the Unity Download Assistant, choose the Unity version and build-support modules you want, and save the files to a real folder (not a temp location) instead of installing immediately — this both downloads everything and generates an `install.bat`. Copy that whole folder to a USB drive, run `install.bat` as administrator on the offline machine, and it installs without touching the network. The one catch: the Editor still needs its license activated afterward, and Unity's "manual activation" method requires generating a request file, taking it to any internet-connected device to submit it on Unity's site, and bringing the resulting activation file back — so the install itself is offline, but activation needs a one-time trip to an online device.

**Unreal: not realistically offline for you.** Epic does have an official "offline installer," but it's gated behind the Developer Portal and only available to organization admins who've purchased Unreal seats or been specifically approved — not something a free/individual Epic account (or a small co-op) can get to. The normal path is the Epic Games Launcher, which streams the download directly (and it's large, 20–100+ GB depending on components) with no public direct-download alternative I could find. Practically, plan on doing the Unreal install over decent internet ahead of time rather than prepping it for offline/USB use, which also lines up with treating Unreal as the optional advanced track in your course.

On the self-containment question, here's how the rest shake out:

Scratch and Godot are both genuinely self-contained — Scratch's installer is one complete package that never phones home to install, and Godot is just a zip with the executable, no install step at all. TIC-80 is the same, a plain zip. GDevelop's Windows installer is a single NSIS-built .exe that installs everything in one shot with no separate download during setup, and there's also an official portable version (extract with 7-Zip, run from anywhere) if you want to skip installation entirely.

GameMaker is the one that isn't self-contained the way you'd want for a USB backup: first-time setup on a new machine requires internet to sign into your account and pull down the runtime, and it re-verifies that account roughly every 30 days whenever it does have a connection. Having the installer .exe on a USB stick doesn't fully solve classroom-wifi problems for GameMaker — the first run still needs to reach the internet.

001 Game Creator's trial (the standalone version, not Steam) looks self-contained for the install step itself, but I couldn't confirm from documentation whether the trial or license activation does a one-time internet check. Since you're already running the licensed copy, your own experience installing it is probably more reliable than what I found — worth just noting what you observed.

Sources:
- [Unity Manual — Install Unity on offline computers](https://docs.unity3d.com/Manual/DeployingUnityOffline.html)
- [Epic Developer Community — Offline Installer of Unreal Engine](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/offline-installer-of-unreal-engine)
- [GameMaker Help Centre — User Permissions and Internet Access Required by GameMaker](https://help.gamemaker.io/hc/en-us/articles/360022953052-User-Permissions-and-Internet-Access-Required-by-GameMaker)

- [Scratch Wiki — Offline Editor](https://en.scratch-wiki.info/wiki/Offline_Editor)
- [001 Game Creator Standalone](https://001gamecreator.com/001-standalone/)

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   This is a long-running session building a homeschool "Learn Programming by Making Video Games" course for SLHE Homeschool Co-op (Robert Kuropkat, robert.kuropkat@gmail.com), Middle/High School students, BYOD, 30 lessons across two semesters, 8 supported engines (Scratch, Godot, Unity, GameMaker, GDevelop, TIC-80, 001 Game Creator, Unreal). This session segment covered, in chronological order:
   - Completing Lesson 2 dual-path (visual/scripting) instruction additions for 4 hybrid engines (GameMaker, Unity, Unreal, 001 Game Creator) in Handouts and Teacher's Keys.
   - Creating and embedding two conceptual diagrams (Game Loop; Sequences vs. Events) into the Lesson 2 Teacher's Script.
   - Creating a Game Design Document (GDD) template pre-populated with real course milestones and student-note space.
   - **User feedback**: "The GDD looks great. Can we add the class branding to it so it matches our Power Point deck from Lesson 1. Also, I don't see the Lesson 2 slide deck or diagrams" — leading to: rebranding the GDD to match the Lesson 1 deck's navy/gold palette and crest, and building a full 17-slide (later 20-slide) Lesson 2 lecture deck that had never actually been created.
   - **User feedback**: "One issue with the diagrams. The image for Events and the image for Game Loop have a problem with the gold arrow heads. They all point right rather than aligning with the tail and pointing at the target box. As for the slides, the look great. If you've not already done so, we should probably save a set of assets/templates for the slide deck and other documents with the branding, etc. and do all of our documents with this matching branding. This may suggest making a template or style sheet for Word docs also. I'd like to go ahead and go back and add that styling to our word docs. Additionally, I'd like to add another set of diagrams. Even though they will be simplistic I think it is a good time to introduce UML like diagrams such as Activity Diagrams (easiest to comprehend) and a state diagrams. Classes I think can come later. Weave these into the slides and lecture notes also." — This required: (a) fixing the arrowhead rendering bug, (b) building a shared branding system (brand.js module + Brand_Style_Guide.docx) and rolling it out to every existing course Word document, (c) creating Activity Diagram and State Diagram for the Key Press Reactor exercise and weaving them into the Lesson 2 slide deck and Teacher's Script.
   - Clarifying questions were asked (via AskUserQuestion) and answered: rollout scope = "Everything (Recommended)"; style guide doc = "Yes, create one (Recommended)"; UML diagram content = "The Key Press Reactor itself (Recommended)".
   - **Most recent user request** (the task in progress when this summary was requested): "Looks really good. I'm not very familiar with Word and PowerPoint, but can we create some sort of template/style sheet or what ever would be appropriate so I can create documents and decks manually with the same deisgn style?" — The user wants actual Word (.dotx) and PowerPoint (.potx) TEMPLATE FILES they can use directly/manually within those applications (not code-generated documents), since they are not technically proficient with Word/PowerPoint. This requires real native template files with pre-configured styles/layouts, plus a plain-language how-to guide since the user is unfamiliar with these apps.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **docx (npm) generation pattern**: shared helper functions (h1/h2/h3/p/bullet/numbered/checkbox/labelBullet/code/headerCell/bodyCell), numbering configs, custom paragraph styles (Heading1/2/3), `styles.paragraphStyles` array registers real Word-recognized named styles usable manually via Word's Style gallery.
   - **pptxgenjs (npm) generation pattern**: `LAYOUT_WIDE` (13.333x7.5in), hex colors without `#`, addShape/addText/addImage/addTable, `bgSlide(dark, darkImg)` full-bleed background image helper (never sets `slide.background` directly — avoids a pptxgenjs 4.0.1 Content_Types.xml defect), `footer(slide, dark, pageNum)`, `pill(slide, text, x, y, w, dark)`, `sectionDivider(icon, title, timeTag, teaser)`.
   - **pptxgenjs 4.0.1 known defects** (confirmed earlier in the project, still relevant): phantom per-slide slideMaster Content_Types.xml overrides (fixed via fix_content_types.py's dynamic orphan-stripping — checks which slideMasterN.xml files actually exist in the package and only removes overrides for non-existent ones, which correctly handles BOTH the simple single-master case AND the new multi-master defineSlideMaster case); malformed notesMaster1.xml with 6 invalid placeholder shapes (always patched to empty spTree); invalid `"oval"` shape preset (must use `"ellipse"`) — not used in this segment's new code but still a standing risk to avoid.
   - **pptxgenjs `defineSlideMaster()` API** (newly researched this session): `pres.defineSlideMaster({ title: "NAME", background: {path}, objects: [{placeholder: {options: {name, type: "title"|"body", x,y,w,h, fontFace, fontSize, bold, color, align, valign}, text: "default prompt text"}}] })`. Creates a real, reusable PowerPoint slide layout. Add a slide using it via `pres.addSlide({ masterName: "NAME" })`. Fill a named placeholder's content via `slide.addText(text, { placeholder: "name" })` (inherits position/font/color from master definition unless overridden). Default placeholder "prompt" text (e.g. "Click to edit title") is UI-only in PowerPoint and correctly does NOT render in LibreOffice PDF export of an unedited slide — confirmed via test_master.js experiment, this is expected/correct behavior, not a bug.
   - **SVG arrowhead rendering bug (root cause, diagnosed and fixed)**: The cairosvg-based SVG→PNG rendering pipeline used throughout this project does not correctly compute `orient="auto"` tangent direction for `<marker>` elements attached to curved (`Q` quadratic bezier) paths — it defaults all such markers to 0° rotation (pointing right), regardless of actual curve direction. Straight-line markers rendered correctly (their direction is trivial to compute), which is why only the curved arrows in diagram_game_loop.svg (all 3 arrows are curved) and diagram_sequences_events.svg (the dashed loop-back curve specifically) were affected — the straight vertical sequence arrows and "yes" arrow were unaffected. **Fix**: replaced all `<marker>`-based arrowheads in both SVGs with manually-rotated arrowhead triangle polygons: `<path d="M0,0 L-11,-4.5 L-11,4.5 Z" fill="COLOR" transform="translate(EX,EY) rotate(ANGLE)"/>`, where ANGLE is computed in Python via `math.degrees(math.atan2(end_y - control_y, end_x - control_x))` (the tangent direction of a quadratic bezier at its endpoint equals the vector from the last control point to the endpoint). All new diagrams (Activity, State) were built using this manual-arrowhead technique from the start, avoiding the bug entirely.
   - **OOXML template conversion technique** (new this session): A `.dotx` (Word template) or `.potx` (PowerPoint template) is structurally identical to a `.docx`/`.pptx` — the only required difference is the `[Content_Types].xml` declaration for the main document/presentation part, changed from `application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.wordprocessingml.document.main+xml` to `....wordprocessingml.template.main+xml` (Word), or analogously `presentationml.presentation.main+xml` → `presentationml.template.main+xml` (PowerPoint, not yet implemented). This makes Word/PowerPoint treat the file as a template: opening/double-clicking it creates a new unsaved document/presentation based on its content, rather than opening the file itself for editing — the correct behavior for a reusable template meant for a non-technical end user.
   - **Stale-file-cache-safe pattern** (established earlier, reused throughout): write to a new incrementing filename before running, rather than re-running an edited-in-place file (e.g., build_lesson02_v4.js → v5.js, build_gdd.js → build_gdd2.js, build_lesson02_teacher_v2.js → v3.js).
   - **Path-mapping bug (self-diagnosed, now resolved)**: The Read/Write/Edit tools' outputs-directory UUID segment is `412acb61-ee76-436a-b740-5bedced3d276` (confirmed via an Edit tool's own error message revealing "your current working directory is..."). I had been mistakenly using `412acb61-ee76-436a-b430-177537aa5542` (confusing it with a different UUID from the knowledge-source project-cache path) for an extended stretch, causing repeated "outside this session's connected folders" Read failures. All Read/Write/Edit calls now correctly use the `-b740-5bedced3d276` prefix. The `mcp__workspace__bash` tool uses a separate, unaffected VM mount path (`/sessions/zen-sleepy-pascal/mnt/outputs/` and `/sessions/zen-sleepy-pascal/mnt/SLHE Programming 2026/`) which was never affected by this bug and remained reliable as a fallback for reading text files via `cat`/`sed`/`grep` when the Read tool was failing.
   - **`pkill` self-matching gotcha**: `pkill -9 -f soffice` matches its own process (since its argv contains the string "soffice"), causing the bash tool call itself to be SIGKILLed (exit 137). Fixed using the classic bracket trick: `pkill -9 -f '[s]office'`.
   - **Shared branding module pattern (`brand.js`)**: A single Node module (`require("./brand.js")`) exporting `NAVY` ("16305C"), `NAVY2` ("1C4A86"), `GOLD` ("C99A2E"), `GOLD_TEXT` ("8A6D1E", darker gold for text-on-white), `TEXT_MUTE`, `CONTENT_WIDTH` (9360 DXA), `FONT` ("Arial"), `stylesBlock` (Heading1/2/3 paragraph styles), `pageHeader(docTitle)` (returns a docx `Header` with "VIDEO GAME CREATION | <docTitle>" right-aligned), `pageFooter()` (returns a docx `Footer` with "SLHE Game Programming" left / "Page N" right via `TabStopType.RIGHT`), `crestParagraph(widthIn, opts)` (centered ImageRun of vgc_crest.png, aspect-locked at 1040/840), `titleBlock(title, subtitle)` (crest + bold navy title + navy2 subtitle + gold "VIDEO GAME CREATION" tag, all centered, returns an array of Paragraphs).
   - **Batch rebranding automation** (`rebrand_batch.py`): A Python regex-based script that transformed 8 near-identical build scripts by (1) injecting `const brand = require("./brand.js");` after the docx require block, (2) replacing inline `new Header(...)`/function-based `pageHeader(text)` calls with `brand.pageHeader("...")`, (3) replacing `new Footer(...)` calls with `brand.pageFooter()`, (4) global string replace `"1B3A5C"`→`brand.NAVY` and `"2E5C8A"`→`brand.NAVY2`, (5) regex-inserting `brand.crestParagraph(1.3, {after:160})` before the first title Paragraph, (6) regex-inserting a "VIDEO GAME CREATION" gold tag Paragraph after the subtitle Paragraph. Produced `*_branded.js` variants for each source script.

Re-rendered via cairosvg, re-embedded into Teacher's Script and Lesson 2 deck, reshipped.

Thinking in that manner, I'd like to define our goals for each level of lesson 02 as such:
Level 01
  - Move sprite right via directional button
Level 02
  - Move sprite right, left, up and down via different, appropriate directional buttons
Level 03
  - Animate sprite when in motion by making it blink while moving and staying static when not
  - Add beep-beep sound while moving, silent when not
  - Change color when moving.  Use a different color for each direction.  Return to original color when not
  - Clamp movement to screen
  - Structure code such that all actions triggered by the same action occur in the same place in code.
Assets required:
  - Use default assets if the exist
  - Use basic shapes if not, or if default sprite does not lend itself well to our need
  - Stretch goal can include changing to a supplied sprite
  - Use default sound editor if exists and is reasonable
  - Use supplied sound effect if no sound editor exists or if using it would be considered well beyond appropriate skill level at this point

Same with color changes. etc.  THAT part does not need to be the same.  However, when all solutions are exectuted, they should blink, beep and move in much the same manner.  Code should be structured in a way that is compliant with the engine best practices and the goals stated above. The peek/poke wiki page confirms nibble-addressing: "To access RAM at byte address 0x4000 you would need to access both the 0x8000 and 0x8001 nibble addresses" - i.e., byte_address * 2 = starting nibble address, explaining the `*2` in `PALETTE_MAP*2+colorIndex`.

It also makes a great Expo display item.  One thing we've not really discussed so far is what kind of game is our mini-game?  I can see two valid options, one is where everyone actually creates the same game for the mini-game then a more personal one for the second semester.  I think of this as similar to "compulsory" routines in Olympic Gymnastics with the second semester being the free form.  However, I can also see how we just make sure the first semester mini-game uses all the same mechanics and techniques but each student gets to personalize it.  I am leaning more towards wanting to make the first semester where everyone designs the exact same game, aka. follows the design we give them.  This will give them a lot of room to still personalize without having to worry about the game "design" while learning the basics of programming and their chosen engine.  Your thoughts?
assistant_text:
Your gymnastics analogy is spot-on, and I'd land where you're landing: same design for Semester 1, personalized for Semester 2.

The strongest argument for it is that it's actually just scaling up something you've already built. Lesson 2's Level 1/2/3 goals are already "same behavior, not same code" — everyone builds the exact same Key Press Reactor, and personalization happens in execution (which engine, how blink/beep/recolor get implemented) rather than in what the thing does. A shared Semester 1 game extends that same philosophy from one lesson to fifteen. You could literally write the mini-game's spec as a Level 1/2/3 goal list, feeding into the same GDD "Goals" table pattern we just built for Lesson 2 — a Semester 1 Capstone Goals table instead of a Lesson N Goals table.

It also solves a real teaching problem: with 8 possible engines and a 1-hour lab, "help me with my thing" from sixteen different game concepts is a lot harder to run than "help me with our thing." A shared design means you can pre-build one vetted asset pack, give concrete debugging help, and write an objective rubric — all things that get much harder once every student's game diverges. And since the class is explicitly "Learn Programming by Making Games," not "learn game design," removing the design-paralysis variable during the semester where they're also learning to program and their engine keeps cognitive load pointed at the actual target skill.

The risk is mainly motivational — some students, especially older high schoolers, might chafe at being told what to build. Two things blunt that: the SuperStretch Ideas doc already gives room to go beyond spec if they want, and the personalization axis you mentioned (skins, themes, tuning, juice) is real ownership even inside a fixed design — it's not nothing. Framing matters too: pitch it as "everyone builds the same game so you can focus on leveling up your coding," not "you don't get to design anything," and land the "this is MY game" moment squarely at the Semester 2/Expo capstone where it belongs.

One real design constraint worth flagging now: whatever mini-game you pick needs to be genuinely buildable at comparable complexity across all 8 engines/platforms — trivial in Scratch shouldn't mean overwhelming in Unreal, or vice versa. That's worth treating as its own design pass.

Want to start sketching what that compulsory Semester 1 game actually is — genre, core mechanic, win/lose condition — the same way we nailed down Lesson 2's goals?

human_text: Yes, I think we should do that.  I know a top down shooter like Space Invaders is a common choice.  it has minimal art and animation requirements while giving room to expand exponentially.  Another is a tower defense type.  My son and I already did Plant's Vs Zombies based on the youtube tutorial that went with this project: https://scratch.mit.edu/projects/761392907/  I'm less inclined to do a platformer or side scroller because I think they will introduce too much wiggle room for a first project
assistant_text:
Space Invaders is the stronger pick, and I'd rule out tower defense for the same reason you ruled out the platformer — it actually has more wiggle room, not less.

A platformer's mess is mostly one system (physics tuning: gravity, jump arc, coyote time). Tower defense stacks several interacting systems at once: a grid/lane placement layer, a currency/economy that accrues over time, multiple unit types with distinct stats, wave-timing and enemy pathing, and a UI for selecting/placing units. That's a lot of surface area to keep uniform across 8 engines with very different native strengths, and the input model is the real problem — click-to-place-and-spend is straightforward in Godot/Unity/GameMaker/GDevelop, native in Scratch's drag-and-drop, but genuinely awkward in TIC-80 (mouse support is limited) and heavier to set up in Unreal (UMG). It's a great game, just not one that stays "comparable complexity" across your whole engine roster.

Space Invaders solves that cleanly, and it's basically a direct extension of what you've already built rather than a new foundation:

Arrow-key movement plus spacebar-to-shoot is the exact same input model as Lesson 2's Key Press Reactor — every engine already handles it identically well, TIC-80 included. And the mechanic progression maps almost exactly onto the milestone table already in the Syllabus and GDD: movement + shooting lands in the Lessons 2-6 programming-foundations window, collision + scoring + win/lose is literally what Lessons 7-11 already say, and enemy waves + audio + basic animation is exactly the Lessons 12-15 game-feel-and-polish window. You wouldn't be inventing a new arc, just filling in the one you already wrote.

Art stays minimal (squares/triangles are fine, sprites are tiny, which also suits TIC-80's constraints well), and there's real room to layer Level 1/2/3 on top: Level 1 is one row of enemies and static shooting, Level 2 adds lives/multiple rows/increasing speed as the formation thins, Level 3 opens up to UFO bonus enemies, barriers/shields, wave progression, whatever a given student wants to chase. Personalization lives in reskinning, tuning, and how far into Level 3 they push — same pattern as Lesson 2, just at capstone scale.

One more thought: PvZ is a fine project, just maybe better saved as a Semester 2 personalized option (or an instructor demo/reference) rather than the Semester 1 compulsory game — partly for the complexity reasons above, and partly because there's already a well-known public tutorial matching it almost exactly, which invites students to just follow that instead of building from your teaching. Space Invaders has plenty of tutorials too, but none that map step-for-step onto your specific 15-lesson arc the way the PvZ one would.

Want me to start drafting the actual mini-game design spec — core mechanic, Level 1/2/3 goals, win/lose conditions — the same way we did for Lesson 2?

Yes, that's a genuinely solid workflow — it's how real production actually runs (high concept → full GDD → production roadmap sliced into sprints), and it also gives you a built-in teaching moment: you can tell students outright "this is how studios actually do this" as you walk them through each layer. It also means Semester 2's personalized projects don't need a new template at all — the living GDD you already built is exactly the "concept → full design → my own milestones" tool for that, just self-directed instead of assigned.

Here's a first pass at the Level 1/2/3 feature breakdown for the shooter, as a starting point to react to:

**Core mechanic:** Player moves along the bottom of the screen and shoots upward to destroy enemies before they reach the player or the bottom of the screen. (Working title TBD — happy to call it whatever, or leave it a codename for now, same as real studios often do.)

**Level 1 (MVP — lands in the Lessons 2-6 window):** Player moves left/right via directional input (direct extension of Lesson 2). Player shoots a single projectile upward on a key press. A fixed row of enemies is on screen. Projectile destroys an enemy on collision. Win condition: all enemies destroyed. That's it — a complete, legitimate finish with zero art or audio requirements.

**Level 2 (Complete — lands in the Lessons 7-11 window, which already says "collision, scoring, win/lose states, simple UI"):** Multiple rows of enemies. Enemies advance toward the player (classic marching formation, or simpler lane-based descent — this is the one design call worth nailing down, since formation-marching is meaningfully harder to build uniformly in block/visual tools than lanes are). Lose condition: an enemy reaches the player or the player is hit. Player has limited lives. Score tracking and a basic score/lives UI. A restart/game-over flow.

**Level 3 (Refined — lands in the Lessons 12-15 "game feel & polish" window):** Increasing difficulty as waves progress. Sound effects (shoot, explosion, game over). Basic animation (explosion flash, hit reaction). Optional stretch features for personalization: destructible barriers/shields, a power-up (rapid fire, spread shot), a bonus enemy for extra points, title/game-over screens.

In theory, this will give us our entire Semester 1 plan with a completed mini-game with the only task remaining to actually test the code samples."

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Standard Level 3 "5-goal" template** (established earlier in the project, being applied engine-by-engine): every engine's Lesson 2 Level 3 content must cover exactly Animate (blink while moving, static when idle), Sound (beep-beep while moving, silent when idle), Recolor (different color per direction, reset when idle), Clamp (keep movement on screen), Structure (group everything triggered by the same action in one place) - "same behavior, not the same code" per engine.
   - **Handout `level3` array**: exactly 5 bullets, in that order, phrased "Animate: ...", "Sound: ...", "Recolor: ...", "Clamp: ...", "Structure: ...".
   - **Key `l3Ideas` array**: exactly 6 entries - the same 5 titled ideas (each with `notes` array + optional `code` array) plus a final "Complete Level 3 solution (all 5 goals combined)" entry with the full combined, runnable code.
   - **Super-Stretch relocation policy**: any Level 3 idea cut from an engine during 5-goal normalization (e.g., diagonal-movement normalization, sprite-facing-direction/flip, exposed tunable variables) must already exist in the generic `Lesson_02_SuperStretch_Ideas.docx` before being removed - verified via `pandoc -t markdown` + grep before each removal.

   - **API-verification discipline**: before writing any engine-specific API claim, verify against official docs (WebSearch/web_fetch) unless the fact is extremely high-confidence/common-knowledge (explicitly reasoned per-case).    a) Completing the standing task of documenting a new "PDF companion" policy (every .docx gets a matching .pdf; GDD is the sole exception where docx remains primary) in Lesson_Production_Standards.docx, then building/shipping Lesson 4's full material set (single enemy + collision detection).

From here on, keep working through the remaining lessons up to and including Lesson 15 without stopping to ask permission at each checkpoint — just keep charging through in the same fast-but-solid style. Only pause and flag me if you hit an actual decision that needs my judgment call (ambiguous requirement, conflicting policy, something you're not confident about) — not just routine 'ready to start the next lesson' check-ins." This instruction governs all work from this point forward: build Lessons 5 through 15 continuously, without asking for confirmation between lessons, only surfacing genuine judgment-call ambiguities.
   c) Building and shipping Lesson 5 (multiple enemies via loops), Lesson 6 (win condition — Level 1 MVP milestone), and beginning Lesson 7 (enemies advance toward the player) per the Feature-to-Lesson Map.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Three Levels of Accomplishment framework**: Level 1 Minimal/MVP, Level 2 Complete/Internal Alpha-Beta, Level 3 Refined/Ready-to-Publish — required for every lesson's exercise, documented per-lesson in a "This Lesson's Goal" tri-state (Plan to Implement/Implemented/Not Planned) checkbox table inside each Lesson_NN_GDD.docx.

   - **Structure principle** (recurring, load-bearing pedagogical theme): an object's own response to events affecting it (being hit, being destroyed) should live entirely inside that object's own script/event, not scattered into the code that detects/triggers the event. This is what allows Lesson 5's loop-spawned enemies and Lesson 6's win-counter to "already work" with zero or minimal new code, and is the direct cause of the Lesson 6→7 bug I identified and fixed in GameMaker/001GC.
   - **Generic-lifecycle-hook pitfall** (the core technical lesson of the Lesson 6→7 transition): GameMaker's "Destroy event" and 001 Game Creator's "Defeated / Destroyed" trigger both fire on *any* destruction of an instance/Actor, regardless of cause. Using them for win-counting (as designed in Lesson 6) silently breaks once a second destruction pathway (escape-off-screen cleanup, introduced in Lesson 7) is added, because the escape path also fires the same generic hook. The fix is to move win-counting logic to the *specific* code path that actually represents "was shot" (the collision/trigger handler), leaving the generic hook to handle only cleanup-adjacent concerns (or removing it if unneeded).
   - **Scratch clone-identity limitation**: Scratch clones have no unique ID; a Bullet clone cannot determine which specific Enemy clone it is touching. The correct fix (introduced in Lesson 5) is to move the touching-check onto each Enemy clone's own script (each clone asks "am I touching a Bullet?" about itself), not the Bullet's script.
   - **Deferred UI philosophy**: Lesson 6's win-text display deliberately uses each engine's most minimal built-in text-drawing tool (Godot Label, Unity OnGUI/GUI.Label, GameMaker draw_text(), GDevelop hidden Text object, TIC-80 print(), 001GC Message Box, Unreal Print String with Print to Screen) rather than a proper UI/Canvas/UMG system, since that's explicitly deferred to Lesson 9 ("Score tracking and a basic on-screen UI").
   - **"Already works for free" pattern**: a recurring Level 2/Level 3 framing device across Lessons 5-6, where good structure from a prior lesson means a new lesson's requirement is satisfied with zero or near-zero new code, explicitly called out and explained (not just asserted) in both Handouts and Keys.

Level 1 MVP milestone complete."), warranting extra celebratory framing in the Teacher's Script, Prep Checklist, and Slides deck (e.g., a dedicated "Milestone Moment" section/slide, an extended share-out at lesson end).

   - **Push vs. Poll** (named explicitly in Lesson 9): two valid strategies for keeping a UI display in sync with data — push (call an update function whenever data changes: Godot, GDevelop, Unreal, 001GC's real-time Field binding) vs. poll (recheck every frame regardless: GameMaker Draw GUI, TIC-80 print(), Unity's new poll-based HUD.cs).

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:

   This is a long-running session building a complete homeschool "Learn Programming by Making Video Games" course for SLHE Homeschool Co-op (Robert Kuropkat, robert.kuropkat@gmail.com), Middle/High School students, BYOD, 30 lessons across two semesters, 8 supported engines (Scratch, Godot, Unity, GameMaker, GDevelop, TIC-80, 001 Game Creator, Unreal). The course follows a "Three Levels of Accomplishment" framework (Level 1 Minimal/MVP, Level 2 Complete/Alpha-Beta, Level 3 Refined/Ready-to-Publish) and a Semester 1 capstone: a compulsory top-down arcade shooter mini-game, tracked via a Feature-to-Lesson Map in `Semester_01_Capstone_GDD.docx`.

   The governing instruction for this entire segment (established prior to this excerpted window, not restated as a new user message within it): "Continue with Lesson 10 and keep working straight through Lesson 15 as instructed — only pause if you hit an actual decision that needs my input." No new user messages occurred during this segment — all work was autonomous execution completing that standing directive. This segment covers: finishing Lesson 11 (Slides deck + GDD + verification), and fully building Lessons 12, 13, 14, and 15 (each lesson's complete 5-file-group: Handouts+Keys+Prep Checklist for all 8 engines, Plan+Teacher's Script, Slides deck, GDD update, and final verification/shipping/MD5-check), completing the entire Semester 1 (Lessons 1-15) buildout.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - **Established 5-file-group build pattern per lesson**: (1) Handouts+Keys+Prep Checklist (8 engines × docx+pdf = 16 Handout files + 16 Key files + 1 Checklist doc+pdf), (2) Plan (1-page) + Teacher's Script (2-3 page), (3) Slides deck (~15 slides via pptxgenjs), (4) GDD goals slice (derived from prior lesson's GDD via targeted, non-blind Python find-and-replace), (5) Verify (PDF render + pdftotext content check) + ship (copy docx+pdf to `Lessons/Lesson NN - Title/` folder structure) + MD5-check (confirm source and shipped copies match byte-for-byte).
   - **Reuse principle**: each lesson's new feature reuses/extends existing code paths. Extended this segment to sound (L12 formalizes L2-6's optional sound ideas), animation (L13's explosion/flash as new self-contained objects following bullets/enemies' established "one object, one job, cleans itself up" discipline), and difficulty (L14's `4 + wave` formula referenced identically everywhere enemy count matters).
   - **Structure principle**: state-changing logic must live in the specific code path representing an event. Extended this segment to: L12's sound calls living inside the exact branch representing their trigger event (no per-frame polling); L13's critical "score/win-check timing is completely unaffected by visual-removal delay" rule, with three engine-family solutions for pausing mid-script (inline await/Coroutine/Wait/Delay for Godot/Unity/GDevelop/Unreal/Scratch vs. split-into-two-events Alarm/countdown for GameMaker/TIC-80 vs. self-timed Flash action for 001GC).
   - **Anti-fabrication research discipline**: dispatched a research subagent (Agent tool, general-purpose type) mid-Lesson-13 to verify real APIs for 001 Game Creator (confirmed "Actor – Flash" and "Spawn Actor"; could NOT verify a dedicated Particle action, so avoided asserting one), GDevelop (confirmed official "Flash" extension and "Tween" behavior), and TIC-80 (critical correction: `pal()` is NOT a real TIC-80 API — matches historical fabrication bug from earlier task #88; confirmed sprite-index-swap via `spr()` as the safe alternative).
   - **Milestone lessons**: Lesson 6 = Level 1 MVP, Lesson 11 = Level 2 Complete, Lesson 15 = Level 3 Refined (Semester 1 Capstone) — all three get identical celebratory slide/document treatment (dedicated Milestone Moment section, special framing, milestone-themed closing).
   - **001 Game Creator's fixed-actor-count constraint turned into a feature** (Lesson 14): since enemies are 5 pre-placed named Actor copies (never runtime-spawned, per Lesson 5 precedent), difficulty scaling via enemy count required adding 2 MORE pre-placed copies (enemy_6, enemy_7) at design time, then gating their revival behind `If(wave >= 2)`/`If(wave >= 3)` in SpawnWave — an honest, confirmed-mechanism-only solution rather than fabricating a runtime spawn API.
   - **Unreal's 3D-primitive track**: confirmed via grep that this course's Unreal track uses basic Cube/Sphere Shape Actors with Dynamic Material Instances (not 2D sprites/Paper2D) — shaped Lesson 13's explosion design (a scaling shape Actor with Timeline-driven material color) and reused the Dynamic Material Instance pattern first seeded in Lesson 3/4's optional visual idea.

Background/nohup processes do NOT persist between bash calls since each call is a fresh isolated environment with no cwd/env carryover.

Workaround: all file creation via `mcp__workspace__bash` heredocs (`cat > file << 'SCRIPT_EOF'`), all verification via `pdftotext`/`pdfinfo`/`md5sum`/`grep` instead of Read.
   - docx-js (via Node, `require('docx')`) and pptxgenjs conventions: unchanged from established pattern — shared `brand.js` module (NAVY/NAVY2/GOLD/GOLD_TEXT colors, `crestParagraph`, `pageHeader`, `pageFooter`), consistent heading/bullet/checkbox/code helper functions, US Letter page size (12240×15840 DXA), LAYOUT_WIDE (13.333×7.5in) for slides with `bgSlide`/`footer`/`pill`/`sectionDivider` helpers referencing pre-existing `bg_title_*.png`/`bg_content.png`/`icons/*.png` assets already present in the outputs/ working directory.

human_text: Does this change affect any of our other lessons for Scratch?  Does it affect any other engines?  With our rule to keep the same features across engines, I don't want to strain any engines natural work flow just to make the code look the same.   While playing around with the Scratch Lesson I realized each implementation might have quirks and not quite work right.  This is okay as these little deviations between engines provides discussion points for the class.
assistant_text:
Checked both questions directly against the actual downstream content rather than guessing:

**Later Scratch lessons (3-15): no impact.** From Lesson 3 onward, every new mechanic (firing, enemies, waves, win/lose, sound, animation) is built as its own new script on the Player/Bullet/Enemy sprites, explicitly called out as "a separate, independent script from your Player's movement scripts" (Lesson 3's language). Nothing downstream reads or depends on how the movement scripts are structured internally — they just call the Player's movement scripts a stable given. The old Level 3 stretch ideas (blink/recolor/bounce) never got referenced again either; every later "color effect" or "blink" mention is unrelated new content on the Enemy or a fresh win/lose cue, not a continuation of Lesson 2's optional ideas. So there's nothing to touch there.

**Other engines: no impact, and no fix needed.** I re-checked the Godot/Unity/GameMaker/GDevelop/TIC-80 solutions, and their "everything in one continuous script" shape isn't the antipattern Scratch had — it's just what those engines' idiom actually is. `_process()`, `Update()`, the Step event, an event sheet, and a main loop are all, by design, "run this every frame" — a single continuous script is the natural way to write them, not something forced on top of a different native structure. Scratch was the outlier specifically because it has real discrete hat-block events as its idiom, and the old solution was fighting that. Worth noting: 001 Game Creator and Unreal are the other two genuinely event/trigger-driven engines on our list (Input Triggers, Keyboard Event Pressed/Released pins), and I found their existing Lesson 2 solutions already use the exact same shape I just built for Scratch — discrete triggers for movement/sound/recolor, one small continuous watcher only for the one thing that needs it (blink). So this wasn't a new pattern I invented, it brought Scratch in line with how its two sibling event-driven engines were already built.

On the "quirks are fine" point — that's already the documented house rule, not a new call: the Standards doc says goals must match across engines (same feature, same input, same result) but implementation should be "whichever way is simplest and most idiomatic for that specific engine," and gives blink/recolor as the explicit example of expected variation. So what you ran into in Scratch is squarely within how this course was already designed to work, not a gap I need to patch elsewhere.

If you hit a specific "doesn't quite work" spot while playing with the new Scratch version, tell me what broke and I'll fix that one directly rather than me guessing at bugs.

assistant_text:
Confirmed — you're not missing anything. 001GC's Input Triggers really do only offer Pressed / Released / Pressed and Released; there's no continuous "while held" trigger type. Continuous movement is handled a different way entirely, via a dedicated event pair:

**Change Movement X** — moves the actor left (-1), right (1), or not at all (0), continuously, using the actor's Speed and Acceleration.
**Change Movement Y** — same, for up (-1)/down (1)/stop (0).

Unlike Position Actor (which nudges the actor once, by a fixed offset, each time the script runs), Change Movement sets an ongoing state that the engine keeps applying every frame on its own until you change it again. So the pattern for "press and hold" is:

- Right Arrow, **Pressed** → Change Movement X to 1
- Right Arrow, **Released** → Change Movement X to 0

Hold the key, it keeps moving; let go, it stops — no loop needed, because the engine's own physics step is doing the continuous part, not your script.

This is exactly how the built-in "Regular Game" Input Set you found earlier on the RPG template does it (that's what that Branch-heavy key-down/key-up script was actually doing — Change Movement +1 on press, and on release, a Branch checking Movement = 1 before zeroing it out). That extra check on release exists because X is one shared value, not per-key: if you're holding Right and tap Left then release it, a naive "set to 0 on release" would kill your still-held Right movement too. Worth keeping in mind once Level 2 has all four keys live, even though Level 1 with just Right Arrow won't hit it.

Our current Handout/Key docs use Position Actor with a fixed offset per press, which only moves once per tap, not while held — so if you want true press-and-hold movement, that's a real content change (swap Position Actor for Change Movement X/Y in Level 1/2, and note the multi-key release caveat for Level 2). Want me to make that switch, or would you rather confirm the feel of Change Movement live first before I touch the docs?

Now, on Position Actor vs. Take Movement in Direction — confirmed from the official events reference:

**Position Actor** directly sets the actor's X/Y coordinates (and map). It's a raw teleport — pixel-based, absolute or relative, no concept of a grid.

**Take Movement in Direction** is built for tile-based games instead: it moves the actor one grid tile in the direction you specify, gliding smoothly into that tile rather than snapping instantly (which is why it pairs well with the "Wait for Movement" event, so a script can wait for that glide to finish before continuing). It's the tile-grid counterpart to Position Actor's raw-pixel approach.

There's also a third option we touched on above — **Change Movement X/Y**, which is neither a teleport nor a tile-step, but an ongoing velocity that the engine applies every frame until you change it again.

So the three are really: Position Actor (instant, any pixel), Take Movement in Direction (one tile, animated), Change Movement X/Y (continuous, velocity-based). You landed on the tile-based one, which makes sense if your Map's using a tile grid — and explains why it worked cleanly for a single press without needing the Change Movement approach we discussed. Good catch on Defined Control, too — that's a nice one for the Super-Stretch list, now added.

assistant_text:
Confirmed — your instinct is right, and there isn't a simpler alternative. `image_blend` is a **multiply**, not a replace: it multiplies the sprite's existing RGB by the color you set, channel by channel. On a pure white sprite that gives you an exact, clean color (white × red = red), but on anything else it genuinely mixes — a blue sprite × red blend gives a dark, muddy result, not clean red. GameMaker doesn't have a built-in "just replace it" property; the two real options are using white/grayscale source art (so multiply behaves like a true recolor) or writing a custom shader for arbitrary recoloring on colored art.

That's actually a bigger deal for us than just GameMaker, though: our placeholder sprites (`player_circle_blue.png`, etc.) are colored, not white, and several other engines' Recolor techniques work the exact same multiply way — Godot's `modulate`, Unity's `spriteRenderer.color`, GDevelop's "Tint color," and 001 Game Creator's recolor system too (its own docs explicitly recommend grayscaling sprites for this same reason). So the Recolor exercise as currently written would look muddy in most of these engines with our actual colored circle art, not just GameMaker.

**2. GameMaker's axis — and it's not the odd one out.** I checked the actual movement code shipped across all of Lesson 2 rather than going from memory. GameMaker: origin top-left of the room, Y increases downward, so `y -= 4` is "up." Godot and TIC-80 use the exact same convention (`position.y -=` for up; `y=y-1` for up) — that's the standard for basically every pixel/canvas-style 2D engine, GameMaker included, tracing back to how screens are scanned (row 0 at the top). The two engines that actually break from that are Scratch (origin at the *center* of the stage, Y increases *upward* — true Cartesian) and Unity (world space is also Y-up). So GameMaker's the norm, not the exception — Scratch and Unity are the ones worth calling out as different. Good Sidebar material either way (see below).

human_text: Ah, I just noticed another question I had forgotten.  In GameMaker, I'm not sure how to implement this code via the visual editor:  var moving = keyboard_check(vk_right) || keyboard_check(vk_left) || keyboard_check(vk_up) || keyboard_check(vk_down);
assistant_text:
GML Visual doesn't have a wire-together boolean node the way Blueprint does — `If Key Down` (the visual equivalent of `keyboard_check`) is a branching action block, not something you can OR together in one expression. So the honest translation restructures the logic as four sequential checks instead of one line:

1. **Assign Variable**: Name `moving`, Value `false` — put this first (top of the Step event), so it resets every frame.
2. Add four **If Key Down** actions (Mouse And Keyboard category), one each for Right, Left, Up, Down — the "Key" dropdown is where you pick the actual key, no "Not" needed.
3. Inside each one's "if" branch — drop the action to the *side* of the If block, not below it, or it runs unconditionally afterward — add another **Assign Variable**: Name `moving`, Value `true`.

End result: `moving` ends up `true` if any of the four are down, `false` if none are — same outcome as the `||` chain, just expressed as four small ifs instead of one wired condition.

One nuance: `Assign Variable` creates/sets an ordinary instance variable, not a `var`-scoped temp one. Functionally identical here since you're using it within the same Step event, but if you want to match `var`'s actual scoping, there's a separate `Declare Temp` action right next to Assign Variable in the Common category that does that — I could confirm the exact page for it, the manual site blocked that specific fetch, but it'll be sitting right there in the action palette if you want to look at it.

Sources:
- [If Key Down](https://manual.gamemaker.io/monthly/en/Drag_And_Drop/Drag_And_Drop_Reference/Mouse_And_Keyboard/If_Key_Down.htm)
- [Assign Variable](https://manual.gamemaker.io/monthly/en/Drag_And_Drop/Drag_And_Drop_Reference/Common/Assign_Variable.htm)

human_text: In GameMaker, is there much of a difference between Assign Variable (X) and Set Instance Variable (X-Coordinate)?  The second seems less "mysterious".  Also, is there a way to use the visual components like Set Direction Fixed or Set Direction Variable and Speed, etc. to accomplish the same thing "more" visually?
assistant_text:
Both confirmed against the manual, and they're a good pair to compare.

**Assign Variable vs. Set Instance Variable:** for a built-in property like x, these do the exact same thing under the hood — same variable, same effect. The difference is entirely in the UI. Assign Variable is the generic tool: you type a name into a blank field, and it works for absolutely anything — a built-in like x, or a custom variable you made up like moving. Nothing stops you from typo'ing "xx" and silently creating a useless new variable instead of moving your instance. Set Instance Variable trades that flexibility for safety: its Variable field is a dropdown of GameMaker's actual recognized built-ins (X Coordinate, Y Coordinate, Direction, Speed, Horizontal Speed, Vertical Speed, Image Blend, and so on) — you can't typo it, and you can see exactly what's available without needing to know it in advance. It just doesn't cover custom variables like moving at all, since the dropdown only lists genuine built-ins. So: "less mysterious" is exactly right, and the tradeoff is a curated, safe menu versus universal-but-unchecked.

**A more visual way to move:** yes, genuinely — and it's not just a style preference, GameMaker's manual frames it as one of the two real ways to move an instance. What this course's Lesson 2 teaches (adjusting x/y directly, `x -= 4`) is one; the other is setting a speed/direction vector instead, via the Movement Actions category — Set Direction Fixed (click one of 8 compass buttons), Set Direction Variable (any angle, 0-360°), Set Speed, or Add Motion. Once speed and direction are set, GameMaker moves the instance by that amount automatically, every step, with no manual x/y math at all.

That's actually a bigger payoff than just looking nicer: GameMaker already tracks a built-in `speed` variable that's automatically nonzero exactly when an instance is actually moving under this system. If movement were built this way, you likely wouldn't need a hand-rolled `moving` variable at all — a single condition check against the built-in `speed` would tell you the same thing.

Worth being honest about the catch, though: this isn't a drop-in visual reskin of what's there now. Setting speed/direction is a continuous, velocity-based way of moving — an instance keeps drifting until something changes its speed again — versus this course's current discrete, one-step-per-press model. Switching to it would actually change how movement feels to play, not just how it's built, which is exactly the "true press-and-hold movement" territory already flagged as a Super-Stretch idea elsewhere in this course (001GC's Change Movement X/Y). So it's a genuinely good thing to know GameMaker supports, but adopting it for Lesson 2 proper would be a real design change, not a free polish pass.

Want me to write this up anywhere — a Level 3 idea, a Sidebar, or just leave it as something you now know for your own use?

human_text: I'm having trouble with another part of the Visual Editor in Game Maker.  We have the if Keydown sequence which is a connected clause.  I added what I had hoped was new if then else structure but it got attached to the Key Down clause.  How do I visually end an if clause if I need to follow it with another if clause?  I was able to place an Assign Variable block to separate them but it seems to me there should be some other correct way to separate two distinct if clasuses
assistant_text:
"Constructing Action Block Code" is exactly the page I need.

Found the exact mechanic in the manual. There's no "end if" block in GML Visual - separation is entirely about *which* highlighted drop zone you release on, not any explicit terminator:

"When using actions that can have a side chain block... the action will have two areas highlighted for dropping further actions: One below the action as normal, one to the right of the action to show that you want to create a separate block of actions to run when the condition of the first action returns true."

So every If-type block (If Key Down, If Variable, etc.) exposes two distinct targets while you're dragging something onto it:

Drop it to the **right** of the If block, and it goes into that If's true-branch - runs only when the condition holds. That's what's been happening to you: your new if/then/else structure is landing on that right-hand zone, so it's getting nested inside "If Key Down" instead of sitting after it.

Drop it **below** the If block itself (aligned with the If block's own left edge, not the indented actions inside it), and it becomes the next step in the main chain - runs unconditionally, after the If block, regardless of whether that condition fired. That's the zone you want for a second, independent If clause.

The trouble is that once an If block already has a few actions stacked inside its true-branch, the "below the last inner action" zone and the "below the whole If block" zone sit very close together vertically, so it's easy to miss and land on the inner one. A few ways to hit it reliably:

Aim for the very bottom edge of the If block's outer boundary, not the bottom of whatever's inside it - the outer edge is usually a bit further down and to the left than it looks.

Watch the Action Overview panel on the left as you hover - it shows the block hierarchy in shorthand and will tell you immediately whether your drop landed as a sibling (same indent as If Key Down) or a child (indented one level deeper) before you even release.

If you do miss, there's no rebuild needed - you can click-and-hold-drag any existing action to reposition it within the chain, so just grab the misplaced If and drag it back out to the correct zone.

Your Assign Variable trick wasn't wrong, it just wasn't the real mechanism - it happened to work because dropping a simple action right after the If block re-anchored a clean "main chain" position for you, which then made it obvious where "below" actually was for the next block. You can pull it back out once you're comfortable placing things directly.

Sources:
- [Constructing Action Block Code](https://manual.gamemaker.io/beta/en/Drag_And_Drop/Drag_And_Drop_Overview/Constructing_Action_Block_Code.htm)

Ah, that fully makes sense — and it's a different (and honestly more classic) gotcha than the one I chased. What you ran into is a scope issue, not a nesting issue.

In GML Visual (same as typed GML), where a variable gets *created* determines whether it survives between steps. Create it once in the Create event with no "Local" flag, and it becomes an instance variable - it lives with the instance for its whole life, so incrementing it in Step actually accumulates frame over frame. But if the first place a variable gets set is an Assign Variable block *inside* Step with its scope set to Local (the visual equivalent of GML's `var`), that declaration re-runs on every single Step call - so the variable gets wiped back to its starting value right before your increment logic even runs. It looks exactly like "the increment isn't working," when really it's working perfectly and then getting erased a fraction of a second later, every frame.

That's actually the same Local-vs-Instance distinction the Lesson 2 Sidebar already touches on for the `moving` variable, just showing up on the "forgot to initialize outside the loop" side of it rather than the "used var when I should've used an instance variable" side. Both fixed and shipped. To directly answer the linking question: GDevelop doesn't have a wiring step at all - there's no connector to draw between a condition and an action. An **event is a single row** with a Conditions side and an Actions side, and that row itself is the entire relationship: everything in the Actions side only fires when everything in the Conditions side is true for that same row. So "linking" a condition to an action just means putting both of them in the same event.

That also means you need **5 separate events** here, not one event holding all your conditions and actions together - one event per direction (Angle of movement = 0/90/180/270) plus one for idle (Is moving = False). If all five conditions end up crammed into a single event, they'd get ANDed together instead of giving you a choice between directions, and nothing would ever fire since an angle can't simultaneously equal 0 and 90 and 180 and 270.

Both docs now spell out the "Add new event, then that event's own Add condition, then that same event's own Add action" sequence, and I fixed the action's name too - "Animation (by name)" is what shows in the picker's search list, it just displays as "Change the animation of Player..." once you've placed it.

Each Event is one row bundling its own Condition(s) and Action(s); an Event's Action(s) only run when ALL of that SAME Event's Condition(s) are true. There is no separate "wiring"/"linking" step — membership in the same Event row IS the link. **Flash visibility (blink) in GDevelop** — it's not a plain action, it's a **behavior**. "Flash object" is an extension that adds a behavior to the object; only after you add that behavior to Player does the **Flash visibility (blink)** action show up in the action picker (search "Flash" under the object's actions once the behavior is attached). Same pattern as "Angle of movement" needing the Top-down Movement behavior — the action lives with the behavior, not with the object by default. Parameters: Object, Behavior, Duration (0 = flash until stopped); a separate **Half period** action/property controls how fast it blinks (default 0.1s), and there's a **Stop flashing visibility (blink)** action plus an **Is object flashing visibility** condition. If the extension isn't already in your project, add it via Project Manager → Extensions → search "Flash".

Sources: [Flash object - GDevelop documentation](https://wiki.gdevelop.io/gdevelop5/extensions/flash/)

human_text: I'm looking at the Scratch solution now.  Default action when the sprite hits the edge is to rotate, or more precisely change the Direction value.  How do I tell it either not automatically change direction or force it back?
assistant_text:
Two ways to handle it, since "if on edge, bounce" changes Direction as its whole mechanism for repositioning the sprite:

**Stop it from changing Direction at all:** don't use "if on edge, bounce." Instead, clamp position directly — check x position/y position against the stage bounds and use "set x to" (not "change x by") to snap it back onto the edge. Something like: if `x position > 230`, set x to 230; if `x position < -230`, set x to -230; same idea for y at 180/-180 (adjust for your sprite's size so it stops before it's half off-stage). This never touches Direction, so there's nothing to flip or rotate — it's the Scratch equivalent of the manual clamp logic other engines use.

**Force it back after the fact:** keep "if on edge, bounce," but immediately follow it with "point in direction [90]" (or whatever direction that script is supposed to represent) to override whatever Direction bounce just set. Bounce still repositions the sprite off the wall, but the direction snaps back right after, so the visual flip never sticks.

There's also a narrower fix if all you actually care about is the visual flip and not the Direction value itself: each sprite has a Rotation Style (the small icons near its direction field, or a "set rotation style" block) — set it to "don't rotate," and the sprite stops visibly rotating/flipping even though Direction still changes underneath. Doesn't touch the actual variable, just the on-screen symptom.

Worth noting: the current Lesson 2 Handout/Key already flag this exact quirk and explicitly punt the "no-flip" fix to a later lesson's position-checking technique — so if you've landed on wanting the manual-clamp approach now instead, that's a real candidate to pull forward. Let me know if you want that changed.

assistant_text:
It's a bit hidden: it's not a separate toggle sitting in the sprite pane by default — you have to click the Direction field itself to reveal it.

In the Sprite pane (top area above the code canvas, where you see the sprite's name, x, y, direction, size, and the show/hide checkbox), click directly on the **direction number** (the compass-style field, defaults to 90). That opens a small popup with three icon buttons: **all around** (rotates normally, the default), **left-right** (flips instead of rotating), and **don't rotate** (third icon) — click that one.

I explained three fix options (force the direction back with a following block, manually clamp position instead of using bounce, or use the per-sprite "don't rotate" rotation-style setting) and researched/found the exact UI location for the rotation-style toggle (click the Direction field in the Sprite pane to reveal a 3-icon popup).

The code you suggested seems to use the legacy Input System, but the current version of unity defaults to the new input system. 2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Unity's Input System: confirmed via official Unity 6.2 manual (docs.unity3d.com/6000.2/Documentation/Manual/Input.html) that "By default, the Input System Package provides input support in Unity... This is the recommended solution for most projects." Legacy `UnityEngine.Input` class (Input.GetKey/GetKeyDown/GetAxis, KeyCode enum) risks throwing InvalidOperationException if Active Input Handling is set to "Input System Package (New)" only; confirmed via a GitHub PR title ("CHANGE: Make 'Both' the default 'Active Input Handling'") that Unity 6 actually defaults new projects to "Both" (legacy AND new system simultaneously active), which is why the course's Unity Visual Scripting altPath content (using legacy-Input-Manager-tied nodes like "On Keyboard Input," "Input > Get Axis") did NOT need to be touched - it still works fine under the "Both" default. The new C# code style adopted: `using UnityEngine.InputSystem;` then direct polling via `Keyboard.current.rightArrowKey.isPressed` (continuous/held) and `Keyboard.current.spaceKey.wasPressedThisFrame` (single-frame/edge-triggered, replacing `Input.GetKeyDown`).
   - Unreal Engine's Enhanced Input System: confirmed via Epic's official docs (dev.epicgames.com/documentation/en-us/unreal-engine/enhanced-input-in-unreal-engine) that Enhanced Input is enabled by default and legacy Action/Axis Mappings are explicitly deprecated since UE 5.1 (with an in-editor deprecation warning banner). Core concepts: **Input Actions** (data assets representing an abstract action like "MoveRight," conceptually equivalent to old Action/Axis mapping names, can be Boolean/Digital, Axis1D/float, Axis2D/FVector2D, or Axis3D/FVector types), **Input Mapping Contexts** (collections mapping physical keys to Input Actions, with Input Modifiers like Negate/Swizzle and Input Triggers), and the requirement to call `AddMappingContext()` via a `UEnhancedInputLocalPlayerSubsystem` (obtained from a Local Player) before any mapped input will actually fire - this step has NO equivalent in the legacy system and is the single most common thing to forget. For C++, confirmed via web search that `"EnhancedInput"` must be added to the project's `[ProjectName].Build.cs` `PublicDependencyModuleNames` array or the subsystem silently fails to register (code compiles, but nothing works at runtime, no compile error). Blueprint binding uses "Enhanced Input Action Event" nodes (right-click, search by Input Action name) with exec pins Started/Triggered/Ongoing/Completed/Canceled - mapped Started↔legacy Pressed, Completed↔legacy Released for this course's discrete-step movement design. C++ binding uses `UEnhancedInputComponent::BindAction(InputAction, ETriggerEvent::Started, this, &Class::Handler)` inside an overridden `SetupPlayerInputComponent()`.
   - Design decision: for the Unreal migration, chose to preserve the course's existing "4 separate discrete Input Actions per direction" structure (IA_MoveRight, IA_MoveLeft, IA_MoveUp, IA_MoveDown, each Boolean/Digital type) bound within one shared Input Mapping Context (IMC_Default) - deliberately NOT switching to Epic's own recommended single-Axis2D-with-modifiers pattern (Negate/Swizzle) for movement, since the existing Level 3 content (blink/recolor/sound/Structure) was built around and explicitly justifies "two different execution contexts" using the 4-separate-events design; switching to a unified axis would have required redesigning already-validated lesson content.

"Build Lighting Only" goes grey when "Allow Static Lighting" is off in Project Settings, which is the normal state for a fresh UE5 project using Lumen (Unreal's default dynamic global illumination). Lumen doesn't use baked lightmaps at all, so there's nothing to build — that button being disabled is expected, not a symptom of anything broken. My auto-exposure/lighting-build advice was a dead end; disregard it.

Since it's not a baked-lighting issue, the real cause is more likely one of these. Two fast checks, in order of likelihood:

First, switch the viewport's shading mode from Lit to Unlit — there's a dropdown at the top-left of the viewport (it may say "Lit"). If the Cube shows up in Unlit but the screen is black in Lit, it's a lighting problem, not a missing-geometry problem. If it's still black in Unlit too, something more fundamental is off (wrong viewport, camera inside geometry, etc.) and that's a different conversation.

Second, if it's specifically a Lit-mode problem, open the World Outliner and check whether a Directional Light actor is actually still there, and if so, check its Intensity in the Details panel isn't 0. It's easy to accidentally delete or nudge that light while dragging the Cube in.

If both of those come back clean (light exists, has intensity, Unlit mode also shows black), it's worth considering that this is a Lumen/hardware issue — Lumen leans on your GPU more than older lighting did, and on weaker or older integrated graphics it can render broken or black rather than just running slow. If that's the case, tell me what GPU your laptop has and I'll look into whether disabling Lumen (switching Global Illumination to a lighter method in Project Settings > Rendering) is the right call for the course generally, not just your machine.
