Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   This is a continuation of a long-running project building a complete Homeschool "Learn Programming by Making Video Games" course (SLHE Programming 2026) for Robert Kuropkat, spanning 8 game engines across a 30-lesson, two-semester curriculum. This conversation segment covers Robert's hands-on testing of Unreal Engine Lesson 2 (and spillover into Lesson 3), with me fixing real, confirmed content/mechanics bugs live as he tests, culminating in a full architectural rewrite of Unreal's Lesson 2 project setup. Specifically:
   a) Added Task #249 tracking Robert's current engine-focus subset (Scratch, Godot, Unity Scripting, GameMaker Scripting, GameMaker Visual, Unreal) vs. eventually validating all engines in all modes (Unity Visual Scripting, GDevelop, TIC-80, 001 Game Creator, Unreal C++).
   b) Diagnosed and fixed a real Unreal Lesson 2 bug chain: (1) Unreal's Blank template auto-possesses a DefaultPawn (flying camera with built-in WASD bindings) on Play, unrelated to the course's Enhanced Input setup, causing unwanted "3D first person" movement and consuming arrow-key input meant for the Cube; (2) fixing this requires a Blueprint-subclassed GameMode (raw/native GameModeBase locks the Default Pawn Class field in World Settings) with Default Pawn Class = None; (3) with no Pawn, the level had no deliberate camera at all, requiring an explicit Orthographic Camera Actor (Auto Activate for Player 0) to get any coherent 2D-style view, with Yaw tuned (confirmed correct at -90) so Right visually reads as screen-right.
   c) Per Robert's explicit direction ("I will probably delete this project and run it from the beginning... This should very definitely be a 2D project from the start and should turn off everything not needed for that"), performed a full architectural rewrite of Unreal Lesson 2's Setup: disable Lumen (GI/Reflection Method = None), delete default Light/Sky actors, create an Unlit Material with a real VectorParameter (not a Constant) so Dynamic Material Instances elsewhere in the course can override it, apply it to the Cube, set Cube Mobility to Movable, set up the no-Pawn GameMode, place and configure the Orthographic Camera, and convert movement from single-press (Started pin) to continuous hold (Triggered pin + Get World Delta Seconds), matching Unity/Godot/GameMaker's established continuous-movement convention. Also audited and fixed downstream Lessons 3, 4, and 13 (BP_Bullet, BP_Enemy, BP_Explosion all needed the same Unlit Material assignment since their default Materials would render solid black with no scene lighting).
   d) Fixed two additional concrete bugs Robert found while rebuilding from scratch: Cube Mobility defaults to Static (needs explicit change to Movable) and Add Actor World Offset's Delta Location pin needs "Split Struct Pin" (right-click) before per-axis values can be wired in — fixed in both Lesson 2 and Lesson 3 (BP_Bullet has the same pattern).
   e) Added a Shift+F1 "release mouse/keyboard focus back to editor" tip per Robert's request, confirmed not already documented anywhere, added to Level1 instructions and a new trouble bullet.
   f) Most recently, fixed three Level 3 (stretch-goal) issues Robert found: (1) "Set Material" node not appearing in Blueprint search (known Context-Sensitive-search quirk; fix is dragging off the Static Mesh Component first or unchecking Context Sensitive); (2) movement sound should be an ongoing repeating beep-beep while held, not a single blip per press (redesigned using a SoundCooldown timer gating Play Sound 2D on the Triggered pin, since Play Sound 2D is fire-and-forget with no persistent "is playing" state to check); (3) confirmed/clarified that Unreal's Material-swapping Recolor approach (5 pre-made flat Unlit Materials swapped via Set Material) already matches the course-wide "swap whole pre-made assets, don't tint directly" design decision established for all other engines — Materials are this track's asset-type equivalent of sprites.

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Unreal's DefaultPawn: a no-gravity, flying-camera Pawn subclass with built-in movement bindings enabled by default (confirmed via Epic's own "Pawn in Unreal Engine" documentation), auto-possessed at Player Start unless Default Pawn Class is set to None.
   - World Settings panel location: Window menu > World Settings (NOT the main toolbar) — confirmed via Epic documentation after an initial wrong guess.
   - GameMode Override in World Settings: sub-fields (Default Pawn Class, etc.) only become editable once GameMode Override is set to an actual Blueprint class; selecting the raw native "GameModeBase" C++ class shows these fields as read-only/locked (confirmed via Epic forum discussion) — the fix is creating a Blueprint Class with parent Game Mode Base, setting Default Pawn Class = None there, then setting that Blueprint (not the raw class) as the GameMode Override.
   - Orthographic Camera setup: standard Camera Actor (not CineCameraActor, which lacks Orthographic support) with Details panel > Camera Settings > Projection Mode = Orthographic and Ortho Width (fixed world-unit width) — confirmed via Epic documentation.
   - "Auto Activate for Player" property on Camera Actor: makes a placed camera the active view for a given player index automatically, with no Pawn possession or Blueprint scripting required.
   - Disabling Lumen: Project Settings > Engine > Rendering > Global Illumination section (Dynamic Global Illumination Method = None) and Reflections section (Reflection Method = None) — confirmed as the single biggest GPU-cost lever for older/integrated-graphics hardware, more impactful than removing the single Directional Light alone.

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:
   This is a continuation of a long-running project building a complete Homeschool "Learn Programming by Making Video Games" course (SLHE Programming 2026) for Robert Kuropkat, an independent game studio founder and homeschool teacher, spanning 8 game engines across a 30-lesson, two-semester curriculum, with 15 lessons (Semester 1) already fully built. This conversation segment covers: (a) shipping a completed Unreal Lesson 2 fix; (b) Robert establishing a new project-wide standing rule ("Rule 5: Engine Deviations Require a Driving Reason") after noticing Unreal's content used flat-color Materials instead of the actual supplied sprite assets used by every other engine, and directing a full audit-and-fix across Lessons 2, 3, 4, and 13; (c) building a new "Cross-Engine Consistency Reference" document cataloging, per lesson (1-15), what components/techniques are meant to stay consistent across all 8 engines and why, flagging inconsistencies found in the process; (d) fixing one of those flagged inconsistencies (Unreal Lesson 7's missing "Split Struct Pin" instruction) and updating the reference doc accordingly; (e) creating a new "Book" folder and a "Book Notes & To-Do" running document as a separate scratchpad (distinct from the main project task list) for the eventual book adaptation of this course, seeded from existing project history; and (f) — the task in progress when this summary was requested — adding a new standing structural requirement for the book (and likely the course's Lesson Production Standards): every lesson/chapter should cover, beyond Level 1/2/3, (1) relevant SuperStretch ideas for that lesson, (2) a "Refinement and Style" section covering code formatting, minor code fixes (e.g., fixing the bullet's initial spawn position), and separation-of-concerns refactors (e.g., moving firing sound from the player script to the bullet script), and (3) for visual-scripting engines, equivalent guidance on node layout/organization and reusing computed values/method calls instead of duplicating them (e.g., calling Get Delta Time once and reusing it). Robert explicitly said to add this as a standing todo item or update the Lesson Production Standards doc (leaving the choice to me), to flag whether the 15 already-completed lessons need a retrofit pass versus applying this only going forward, and explicitly instructed: "don't start the retrofit yet, just scope it."

2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Established build/verify/ship pipeline (used throughout): edit/create a `.js` build script in `Brand_Assets/Build_Scripts/`, copy the script plus `brand.js` and `vgc_crest.png` to a scratch directory under `/sessions/zen-sleepy-pascal/mnt/outputs/`, run `node build_X.js`, convert to PDF via `python3 /sessions/zen-sleepy-pascal/mnt/.claude/skills/docx/scripts/office/soffice.py --headless --convert-to pdf`, verify content via `pandoc -t markdown` + grep (noting pandoc escapes underscores as `\_`, which can cause false-negative greps on names like `M_Player_Red`), visually verify via `pdftoppm -jpeg` + Read tool on rendered page images when layout/formatting matters, copy both `.docx` and `.pdf` to the shipped lesson/doc folder, and `md5sum` both source and shipped copies to confirm byte-identical.
   - Rule 5 (new Standards doc rule, this session): engine content may only deviate from the shared standard form for (1) technical deficiency or (2) genuine engine-norm mismatch requiring an unreasonable workaround — never because a substitute is merely "close enough." Consistency across engines rated as high-value in itself for a multi-engine class.
   - Unreal Material architecture redesigned this session: Unlit Shading Model materials built from a Texture Sample node (RGB → Emissive Color) using imported placeholder PNG assets, sometimes multiplied by a VectorParameter (Color, default White) for genuine per-instance tinting (used for Enemy/stripe-variety/Recolor-via-tint cases), versus separate flat pre-made Materials swapped via Set Material (used for Player Recolor and Enemy-flash "swap to a different real sprite" cases). Critical distinction reinforced: multiplying a Color parameter by White against an already-White-default parameter is a documented no-op (can't produce a true white flash on a colored sprite) — this exact trap already existed in the course's own Godot/Unity/GameMaker instructional text as a known pitfall, and Unreal's original content had NOT been checked against it before Rule 5 existed.
   - Masked vs. Translucent vs. Opaque Blend Mode in Unreal Materials: Masked needed for the Explosion sprite to render its transparent background correctly (hard alpha cutoff via Opacity Mask); Translucent would be needed for a smooth fade-out stretch goal (not the base implementation).
   - Plane Static Mesh vs. Cube/Sphere: chosen for BP_Explosion as the natural flat-quad fit for a 2D sprite viewed by the established top-down Orthographic Camera (from Lesson 2's Setup).
   - "Split Struct Pin" Blueprint quirk: Add Actor World Offset's Delta Location pin starts collapsed as one Vector pin and must be right-click-split before wiring a value into just one axis — a recurring gap first found/fixed in Lessons 2 and 3 in an earlier session segment, newly confirmed missing in Lesson 7 this segment (Task #254, partially resolved).

- Drag it in the 2D viewport, or type values straight into Transform > Position in the Inspector.
- For a typical viewport, something like (400, 500) for Player near the bottom and (400, 100) for Enemy near the top is a reasonable starting point — adjust to your actual window size.

That's the WYSIWYG placement the lesson intends — no code needed, and what you see in the editor is exactly what you get at runtime. Worth noting: this only matters for Enemy this week — starting next lesson, Enemy's position becomes fully code-driven (a spawn loop), so the manual placement is a one-week concern for it. human_text: Checking UNity now.  Unity has the same issue with shounds and object destorying as Godot, but the instructions (Teacher's Key) does not include the same process to hide wait and destory so the sound plays
assistant_text:
Unity's Key isn't actually missing that protection — it just solves the same problem a different way. `AudioSource.PlayClipAtPoint(hitSound, transform.position)` is a static method that spawns its own temporary, independent audio source and self-destroys when the clip finishes — it doesn't live on the Bullet or Enemy at all, so destroying either object immediately after has zero effect on whether the sound finishes. That's Unity's idiomatic answer to the exact problem Godot solves with hide+await+queue_free. So no gap there.

But checking this did surface something more significant: in Unity (and GameMaker, GDevelop, TIC-80 — I checked all of them), the **Bullet** detects the hit and owns the whole response — destroy both, play the sound. In Godot, it's backwards: the **Enemy** detects the hit (via its own Hitbox's `area_entered`) and owns the response. That's not just a sound-handling difference, it's the actual Structure goal pointing in opposite directions depending on engine — exactly the kind of inconsistency Rule 5 exists to catch, and I don't see a technical reason for it: Bullet already has its own Hitbox Area2D too (added in the same Setup step), so connecting *its* signal instead would work exactly the same way in Godot.

The fix itself is contained — move the `area_entered` connection from Enemy's Hitbox to Bullet's Hitbox, and have Bullet's handler call a method on Enemy (still emitting `destroyed` and calling `queue_free()` internally) instead of Enemy detecting it directly. Since Lessons 5-14 all just listen for Enemy's `destroyed` signal regardless of what triggers it, this shouldn't cascade into rewriting those — but I'd want to actually check each one before promising that.

Given this touches already-shipped Lesson 4 content and I want to verify the downstream lessons cleanly before touching anything: want me to go ahead and fix it now, or would you rather I just log it as a flagged inconsistency (Cross-Engine doc / Book Notes) and take care of it later?

human_text: l solved this by what I consider seperation of concerns.  I gave both the enemy and the buillet a hitbox (or collider in Unity) and let each one destroy itself rather than one trigger doing both.  I then attached the explosion (hit) sound to the enemy trigger.  I did not notice the way you did the audio clip in Unity.  I will go back and do that as you designed and check it. (I used audio source instead of audioclip)
assistant_text:
That's a genuinely good design — cleaner than what's actually in the Handout/Key right now, everywhere, not just Godot. Both Bullet and Enemy already get their own Hitbox/Collider in every engine's Setup this week, so the infrastructure was already there; the current Keys just have one side reach over and destroy the other, which means Bullet has to "know about" Enemy (or vice versa) to kill it. Each side detecting its own hit and destroying only itself avoids that entirely — no cross-object reaching, better encapsulation.

On the sound: your instinct is right, and it's worth being explicit about why. `Destroy()` (and Godot's `queue_free()`) are deferred to the end of the current frame, not instant — but "end of frame" still comes well before a hit sound finishes playing. An AudioSource that's a child of Enemy gets torn down along with Enemy in that same frame regardless, so it'll still get cut short. `PlayClipAtPoint` sidesteps that by spawning a completely detached audio object that isn't a child of anything you're about to destroy — that's the actual reason it survives, not just "it's a different API."

Worth flagging: this "each side destroys only itself" pattern is different from what's actually written in Lesson 4's Handout/Key for every engine right now (they all have one side detect the hit and destroy both). Since it's a real improvement — and it happens to line up naturally with sound placement too — do you want me to update Lesson 4 across all 8 engines to teach this as the standard pattern, or are you just running with it for your own build and leaving the shipped course content as-is?

human_text: I am testing unreal right now and could use some help with the editor manipulation.  When I vew the Level there is a a camera setting at the top that says perspective.  It makes moving around in there a pain.  I really don't want to see my game objects as cubes and I really don't want to rotate the view and other nonesense.  Is there a way to make that view in the editor a plain 2d ortho view so I don't keep jacking up the camera view?  I would also like it to default (or be able to quickly put it back) to view my entire game screen rather than being zoomed in on one player.  Also, it seems the background is some sort of composit thing because I keep clicking in it and it single rectangle is shows selected and suddenly I am deep in the Landscape portion of the outliner. assistant_text:
Three separate things here — let me take them one at a time.

**Perspective → Top orthographic:** at the top-left of the viewport toolbar there's a dropdown literally labeled "Perspective" — click it and choose **Top**. That alone also kills the accidental-rotation problem: orthographic views don't support orbit/rotate at all, so right-click-drag just pans instead of spinning the camera around. Once you switch to Top, there's nothing left to "jack up." This should stick between sessions too — viewport camera mode is an editor layout preference, not something saved in the level file, so it won't reset back to Perspective next time you open the project (unless you reset your editor layout).

**Getting back to a full-play-area view on demand:** two tools work together here —
- Select the actors that bound your play area (Player, Enemy, camera markers, whatever), then press **F** — that frames/zooms the viewport to exactly fit whatever's selected.
- Once you've got that Top view framed exactly how you want it, press **Ctrl+1** (or any number 0-9) to save it as a camera bookmark. From then on, just tap **1** (no Ctrl) any time your view has drifted, and it snaps straight back to that exact framing. This is the "quickly put it back" button you're looking for.

**The Landscape:** that's almost certainly a Landscape actor — Unreal's terrain system, which splits itself into many small components/proxies for streaming efficiency. That's exactly why clicking one spot selects a tiny piece and buries you deep in a nested Outliner hierarchy instead of one clean object. You're right that it's dead weight for a flat 2D top-down game — it does cost real rendering/streaming overhead for something that isn't even visible under an orthographic top-down camera. Don't fight it by clicking in the viewport: use the search box at the top of the World Outliner panel, type "Landscape," select the actual top-level Landscape actor from that filtered list, and delete it outright (Delete key or right-click > Delete).

One thing worth checking: the Handout's Setup step 1 says to create the project from the **Blank** template specifically — Blank shouldn't ship with a Landscape by default (just a simple floor, a Directional Light, and a Sky Atmosphere/Sky Light, which Setup already has you delete). If you're seeing a Landscape, it's worth double-checking which template got picked when the project was created — if it was something other than Blank, there may be other unwanted default content riding along with it too, not just the terrain.

Since fighting Perspective navigation is basically a universal first-five-minutes pain point in Unreal for a 2D course, want me to add a quick viewport-setup note (Top view + bookmark trick) to the Unreal Setup steps so future students don't have to ask this same question?

human_text: Yes on that Viewport setup.  Also, I am **pretty** sure I selected the blank project but it definately defaulted to 3D.  If there is other cruft I should search for and delete, lets make a list so we can lighten this up.  Finally, the Top camera worked great (duh) with one exception.  "Above" is now to the right.  So when I placed my enemy "above" the player in the perspective view and switched to the top view, it now shows to the right with is counter intuitive
assistant_text:
**The "above shows as right" mystery:** this isn't the Top view's fault — it's the Camera Actor's rotation. Back in Setup, you set that camera to Yaw = -90 specifically so "Right" would read as screen-right during actual gameplay (per the Trouble note about adjusting Yaw in 90° steps). But the editor's plain Top orthographic view has its own fixed, unrotated convention (world +X = screen-up, +Y = screen-right) that has nothing to do with your Camera Actor's rotation — it's just the editor looking straight down, always the same way, regardless of any camera you've placed. Once you rotated the actual gameplay camera 90° to fix left/right for players, that same 90° is exactly what now separates "up" in the plain Top view from "up" as players will actually see it. That's not a coincidence — it's the direct cost of the earlier fix.

The clean solution: don't eyeball placement in the generic Top view — **pilot your actual Camera Actor** instead. Select it (Outliner or click it in viewport), right-click, and choose **Pilot 'YourCameraName'**. The editor viewport then locks to that camera's exact position and rotation — you're literally looking through the same camera the game uses, so "up" in the viewport is "up" for the player, guaranteed, no mental rotation math required. There's a "Stop Piloting" button that appears to hop back out when you're done.

**On the cruft:** you probably did pick Blank correctly — "Blank" in Unreal means no gameplay framework, not an empty level. It still ships with a basic default scene. Worth checking the Outliner (same search-box trick as the Landscape) for these, since none of them do anything for a flat Unlit 2D game and some cost real rendering overhead:

- **Post Process Volume** — color grading/exposure/bloom; irrelevant to Unlit materials, safe to delete.
- **Exponential Height Fog** — atmospheric fog, purely visual overhead with nothing to fog here.
- **Nav Mesh Bounds Volume** — AI pathfinding data structure; you're not using AI navigation.
- **Floor** (a plain Static Mesh) — harmless to leave, but since your "ground" is really just an Unlit black background behind your sprites, you could delete it too if it's not doing anything useful.
- **Player Start** — harmless either way, since BP_NoPawnGameMode never spawns a Pawn to use it.

Landscape is the one actually worth flagging as unusual for Blank specifically — the rest above are just normal Blank-template scenery you don't happen to need.

Want me to fold all three of these (Top view + bookmark, the Pilot-camera tip for placement, and this cruft checklist) into the Unreal Setup/Trouble content in one pass?

human_text: so new project->games->blank has a quality preset with choices of maximum and scalable.  should i select scalable?
assistant_text:
Yes, go with **Scalable**. That preset targets a broader range of hardware (including older/integrated-graphics laptops) and starts with lighter default rendering settings — lower shadow quality, no assumption of ray tracing hardware, etc. "Maximum" targets high-end desktop/console GPUs and turns on the expensive stuff (Lumen, Nanite, high-fidelity shadows/reflections) by default. That's exactly backwards from what this course needs — Setup already has you manually switching off Lumen and reflections afterward anyway, and Scalable means fewer heavy defaults fighting you before you even get there.

One honest caveat: I don't think Quality Preset is what controls whether a Landscape/HLOD/World Partition setup gets included in the default level — that's more likely tied to the template or engine version itself, not this rendering-quality toggle. So Scalable is the right call for performance, but it may or may not sidestep the Landscape situation. Worth just checking the Outliner again once the project's created, same as before.

Multiple sources (including Epic's own developer forums, with a thread literally titled "blank project has landscape, light and so on, but why?") confirm that Unreal's "Blank" project template genuinely does ship with a default Landscape, lighting, and sky despite the name — it's not actually blank, it's just misleadingly named. That's independent of World Partition, too: in UE5, *every* new level has World Partition enabled by default, project template aside — so even a truly clean level would carry some World Partition scaffolding, it just wouldn't have a Landscape or HLODs generating against it.

The practical fix for what you have now: instead of cleaning up the level that ships with the project, go **File → New Level → Basic** (not the default one) — that gives you a genuinely minimal level (a simple floor plus basic lighting, no Landscape), delete the floor too if you don't want it, and work from there. Enable it via **Edit → Plugins**, search "Paper 2D," enable, restart the editor. Once on, it gives you actual 2D-native asset types — **Sprites** (import a PNG directly, no Material/Texture-Sample wiring needed), **Flipbooks** (sprite-sheet animation), and **TileSets/TileMaps** for level layout. That's notably closer to how every *other* engine in this course already works (Godot's Sprite2D, Unity's SpriteRenderer, GameMaker's sprites) than the current Cube+Unlit-Material approach, which has needed a fair amount of manual Material/Texture-Sample setup to fake what a Sprite asset gives you for free.

That said, switching to Paper2D would be a real redesign, not a tweak — it'd touch the underlying actor/asset type across every Unreal lesson already built (2 through 15), not just the project-creation step. Worth you trying it hands-on first — spin up a quick throwaway test, enable the plugin, import a sprite, get a feel for the workflow — before we talk about whether it's worth adopting course-wide. human_text: So some questions in fixing our current project.  When I select new level, I have four choices, Open World, Empty Open World, Basic and Empty Basic.  Can you tell me what the difference is between the last two?  It sounds like Empty Basic would be the better choice to even Basic?
assistant_text:
Your instinct's right — **Empty Basic** is the better pick. Here's the actual difference:

- **Basic**: floor plane + lighting + atmosphere + exponential fog already placed for you.
- **Empty Basic**: nothing at all — no floor, no lights, no atmosphere, no fog. A genuinely blank canvas; you add everything yourself.
- **Open World / Empty Open World**: these are the ones actually built around Landscape + full World Partition streaming, meant for large-scale terrain projects — skip both for this.

Since your Setup already manually builds up everything you actually need (Camera, Materials, Input Actions) and already has you delete the default Directional Light/Sky Atmosphere/Sky Light rather than keep them, Empty Basic matches that philosophy exactly — you'd skip deleting Basic's floor/lighting/atmosphere/fog by hand since none of it would be there in the first place. Go with Empty Basic.

   - Unity's `AudioSource.PlayClipAtPoint(clip, position)`: a static method that spawns its own temporary, independent audio-source GameObject which self-destroys once the clip finishes playing — functionally equivalent to Godot's more manual "hide + disable Hitbox + play + await finished signal + queue_free()" pattern for surviving object destruction, but achieved via a completely different (simpler, Unity-idiomatic) mechanism. Key nuance: `Destroy()`/`queue_free()` are deferred to end-of-frame (not instant), but this does NOT save a child AudioSource/AudioStreamPlayer from being destroyed along with its parent in that same frame — the "detached, independent object" pattern (PlayClipAtPoint or Godot's manual equivalent) is what actually solves the cutoff problem, not the deferred-destruction timing itself.
   - Cross-engine Lesson 4 hit-detection inconsistency (flagged, deliberately NOT fixed in shipped content): Unity/GameMaker/GDevelop/TIC-80 all have the **Bullet** detect the collision and destroy BOTH objects (asymmetric ownership); Godot's shipped content has the **Enemy** detect and destroy both (opposite asymmetric ownership). Robert's own project uses a third, better pattern: **Bullet and Enemy each independently detect their own hit and destroy only themselves** — no cross-object reaching, cleaner separation of concerns. Robert deliberately chose NOT to retrofit this into any shipped Lesson 4 content, reserving it as future "Rule 6 Refinement and Style" / book Sidebar material tied to a "who's in charge" concept he's already introduced verbally in class.
   - Unreal Engine editor navigation: Level Viewport's "Perspective" dropdown (top-left of viewport toolbar) can be switched to "Top" for a fixed orthographic view; orthographic views disable orbit/rotate entirely (right-click-drag pans instead). Press **F** with actor(s) selected to focus/frame the viewport on them. **Ctrl+[0-9]** sets a camera bookmark at the current viewport transform; pressing the bare number **[0-9]** afterward snaps back to it instantly.
   - Unreal Landscape actors under **World Partition** (enabled by default on every new UE5 level, regardless of project template) are split into many small "Landscape Streaming Proxy" actors for streaming efficiency — there is no single clickable "parent" actor to select/delete via ad hoc viewport clicking; proper removal is through **Landscape Mode** (Modes dropdown > Landscape > Manage tab). 2. Key Technical Concepts:
   - Unreal Engine New Level templates: Basic (floor/lighting/atmosphere/fog pre-placed) vs Empty Basic (genuinely empty) vs Open World/Empty Open World (Landscape + World Partition, avoid for this project).
   - Blueprint Classes are separate, portable assets independent of Level; Level Blueprint content (variables, actor references) is level-scoped and does NOT survive a level swap — the central architectural lesson driving the whole rebuild.
   - Unreal Collision system: Collision Presets (BlockAllDynamic vs OverlapAllDynamic), Generate Overlap Events, Collision Enabled (Query Only), Sweep parameter on movement nodes (Add Actor World Offset/Set Actor Location) — without Sweep, no collision testing occurs during a move at all.
   - Component hierarchy: native-inherited root components (Category: StaticMeshActor, from parenting a Blueprint Class directly off Static Mesh Actor via "New Subclass") vs manually-added components (Category: Default, from "Blueprint Class (Actor parent) + Add Component"). The real root cause of Robert's collision bug was a component with Static Mesh field = None while a nested orphan "Cube" child held the actual mesh — NOT the Default Scene Root hierarchy (that fix was tried and confirmed NOT necessary).
   - Auto Receive Input: a plain (non-Pawn) Actor Blueprint does not receive keyboard input at all unless Auto Receive Input is set (Class Defaults, Input category, set to Player 0) — critical difference from Level Blueprint, which receives input for free.

That's the real bug, and it traces back further than Lesson 5. I had it fully investigated — here's what's actually going on:

**Root cause:** Lesson 4 built Bullet's and Enemy's `Hitbox` (Area2D) with no Collision Layer/Mask setup at all — the Setup steps just say "add an Area2D... with a CollisionShape2D sized to roughly match the sprite," and every `Area2D` in this course is left on Godot's default `Layer 1 / Mask 1`. On top of that, the hit-response handler never checks what actually entered:

```gdscript
func _on_hitbox_area_entered(area):
    area.get_parent().queue_free()
    queue_free()
```

It fires identically whether `area` belongs to a Bullet or another Enemy. In Lesson 4 this never showed up because only one Enemy ever existed at a time. Lesson 5 is the first time multiple Enemies exist near each other, and at 128×128px sprites spaced only 60px apart on X, adjacent Hitboxes overlap — so each Enemy's Hitbox detects its neighbor's Hitbox, and both self-destruct. Lesson 5's own Level 2 claim ("this already works with no extra code... every instance behaves independently") is actually false as currently written.

There are two real fixes, and they're not equivalent:

1. **Widen the spacing** (e.g. 60→150+) so hitboxes never touch. Quick, but it's a patch, not a fix — the underlying issue (Enemy can "hit" Enemy) is still there and would resurface the moment spacing, sprite size, or a future denser layout changes.
2. **Fix the actual gap**: give Bullet and Enemy distinct Collision Layers in Lesson 4 (e.g. Bullets on layer 2, Enemies on layer 3) and set each Hitbox's Mask so it only detects the layer it's supposed to react to — or, cheaper to teach, add a group check (`area.is_in_group("bullets")`) in the handler before treating it as a hit. This is the structurally correct fix and also teaches something Godot students need eventually anyway, but it means revising Lesson 4's Setup/Level 1 solution (not just Lesson 5), since that's where Hitbox was first built.

Given this project's own standing rule against papering over root causes with workarounds, I'd lean toward option 2, done in Lesson 4 where the gap actually originates, with Lesson 5 then correctly claiming Level 2 "just works." But this touches two lessons' Handout/Key/possibly Teacher's Script, so I didn't want to start editing without your call.

Since you made me look at the Godot Debugger I realized I had silently been getting some warnings.  This is becaause I left some default functions in.  For now I fixed them with the recommended underscore prefix and left the functions themselves in case we need the later.  I'm just curious though what this leading underscore in the argument list of a function does?

W 0:00:01:264   GDScript::reload: The parameter "delta" is never used in the function "_process()". If this is intended, prefix it with an underscore: "_delta".
  <GDScript Error>UNUSED_PARAMETER
  <GDScript Source>main.gd:17 @ GDScript::reload()
assistant_text:
In GDScript, a leading underscore on a parameter name is purely a signal to the static analyzer, not a language feature with runtime behavior. `delta` and `_delta` work identically — same value, same scope. The underscore just tells the parser "I know this parameter is unused, don't warn me," which suppresses that exact `UNUSED_PARAMETER` warning.

It's the same idea as Python's convention of naming an unused loop variable `_`, just applied to function parameters specifically. Worth knowing: Godot uses the same underscore-prefix convention in a couple of other unrelated spots too — a leading underscore on a *method or variable name* (like `_ready()`, `_process()` themselves) is Godot's virtual/engine-called-function marker, and a leading underscore on your own variable/method names is a weak "treat this as private" convention (not enforced, unlike GDScript's real `@export`/access rules). Different meaning each time, same character — worth flagging to students if this comes up, since it's an easy thing to conflate.

Summary:
1. Primary Request and Intent:

   This is a long-running project building a homeschool game-programming course ("SLHE Programming 2026" / "Video Game Creation") for Robert. This conversation segment covers six sequential threads:

   a) **Carried over from prior summary**: Complete Task #330 (rebuild/verify/ship all Lesson 5 GameMaker-affected files: Handout, Key, Lesson_Production_Standards.docx, Book_Notes_and_ToDo.docx) — fully completed, including the final PDF visual spot-check, shipping, and MD5 verification. Explicitly NOT fixed since it's a shared asset across all 8 engines and only GameMaker has been retrofitted to Rule 11 so far.

   b) Robert asked to be reminded, after he reviews the Godot and Unity Lesson 5 documents, to decide whether to extend the Rule 11/ternary-removal changes there too. I updated Task #331 to reflect "on hold" status pending that review.

   c) Robert reported a real bug: "Code for Godot is not working. No enemy appear. They are neither on the screen nor in the Renote Scene tab during play." Through iterative diagnosis (his own testing plus my research into Lesson 3/4 Godot's collision architecture), we determined: Godot's Hitbox `area_entered` handler has zero type-check on what triggered it, and at the original 60px spacing with 128×128px sprites, adjacent Enemies' hitboxes overlapped and mutually destroyed each other. Robert independently confirmed this ("The placement is bad. They are too close to each other and 'colliding' happens too fast to see... When I increased the loop to 2, they disappeared and I actually heard the destroy sound") and provided his own chosen fix: `e.position = Vector2(150 + i * 200, 50)` (widen spacing only, explicitly declining the deeper collision-layer/group-check architecture fix for now). I implemented, verified, and shipped this (Task #332, completed).

   d) Robert then revealed Scratch has the identical problem (overlapping clones causing double-hits, not full destruction) and that he'd already fixed it himself: "I adjusted the values for Enemy_x to be enemy_number * 100 - 300" — also renaming the loop variable from `enemy_i` to `enemy_number` (consistent with the Rule 11 naming philosophy established earlier in the session). He also asked me to identify the right lesson to formally teach collision-type filtering (Bullet vs Player vs Enemy vs Enemy), framing it as "Now our enemies are moving around, they can collide with each other AND the player. How do we fix this?" I researched Lessons 6–15's actual content and found that true Player-vs-Enemy touch collision never appears anywhere in Semester 1 (only Bullet-vs-Enemy from Lesson 4, and an escape-based life-loss in Lesson 8) — deferred explicitly to Semester 2's AI/movement unit per Lesson 15's own teacher script. I presented this finding via AskUserQuestion with two options (split enemy-vs-enemy into Lesson 7 now vs. hold the whole topic for Semester 2); Robert chose: **"Let's go with option 2, Hold the whole topic until Semester 2, but just make sure we silently ensure it is not a problem."** This led to: (1) fixing Scratch's Handout+Key with the enemy_number rename and new formula (Task #333, completed), and (2) a full Semester 1 audit (Task #334, completed) of all remaining engines' collision architecture, which found only 001 Game Creator is vulnerable (generic "Collided with actor" trigger, no type check) — Unity, Unreal, GDevelop, and TIC-80 are all safe by design. For 001GC, I quietly strengthened placement instructions (no new pedagogical text) in Lesson 5 Handout+Key ("at least a full enemy-width of empty gap") and Lesson 14 Handout+Key (same gap guidance for newly-added enemy_6/enemy_7), and corrected a factually-incorrect claim in Lesson 7's Teacher's Key (instructor-only, not shown to students) about "Collided with actor" being "inherently specific" — all built, verified, shipped, MD5-checked.

   e) Robert asked a conversational, non-task question about a Godot Debugger warning he'd seen: `The parameter "delta" is never used in the function "_process()". If this is intended, prefix it with an underscore: "_delta".` — I answered directly (no tools) explaining the underscore is a pure static-analyzer signal with zero runtime effect, distinct from GDScript's separate "private" naming convention. Robert then said: **"Go ahead and make it a sidebar. Mention 'you might have seen this warning in the debugger. Here's how to fix it and what it means'. Include a short description on 'coding conventions' vs compiler enforced rules, vs static analyzers/lint carping. No need to explain what a public vs. private method or variable is yet, just that these conventins exist to help distinguish them"** — I researched, found no lesson's shown Godot code actually triggers this warning from following the docs exactly, chose Lesson 7 (Godot's demo-rotation lesson, already Sidebars-covered, thematically adjacent existing topic) as the home, wrote and shipped a new sidebar topic (Task #335, completed).

   f) **Most recent, in-progress request**: Robert said: **"Also, I do want to start using better named variables as rule with a ToDo to retrofit earlier lessons eventually, and/or opportunisticly as we go along. Here is the proposed code function with names consistent with our GameMaker work: [code below] ... Make this change to all of Lesson 05 and onward as we test. eg. when I start each new lesson, run a quick pass to update variable names accordingly."**

   His exact proposed code:
   ```gdscript
   func _ready(): 
   	for enemy_count in range(5): 
   		var new_enemy := enemy_scene.instantiate() 
   		new_enemy.position = Vector2(150 + enemy_count * 200, 50) 
   		if enemy_count % 2 == 0: 
   			new_enemy.modulate = Color(0.8, 0.1, 0.2) 
   		else: 
   			new_enemy.modulate = Color(0.95, 0.4, 0.5)
   		add_child(new_enemy)
   ```
   This renames Godot's loop variable `i` → `enemy_count` (used directly as the for-loop iterator, not a separate counter), renames `e` → `new_enemy`, and replaces the ternary color expression with a full if/else block. This is Task #336, currently in_progress — the build/verify steps are done; shipping, MD5 verification, cleanup, Book Notes ToDo update, and final report to Robert remain.

First, we need to make sure Lesson 07 docs comply with all our current rules such as consistent and meaningful naming conventions, increased use of diagrams (uml-like activity and state), consistent structure and increased verbosity on visual coding descriptions, including, if needed visual mockups. Lesson 06 has already happened for this class, but that does not preclude fixing it in Lesson 06 and adding a call-out in the lecture to go back and revisit if that is the better place to do so."*

   - Standards Rules 1-12 (established in prior segments) plus the new **Rule 13: "Shared State Lives on a Dedicated Manager Object"** (added this segment) — codifies that shared/session-level state (win-tracking, score, lives, wave number, etc.) should live on a dedicated manager-style object per engine where the engine's object system supports it, named "GameManager" (or the engine's idiomatic equivalent), with reporting objects (e.g., an enemy) only ever reporting, never counting/deciding/drawing themselves. Documents a Rule-5-style exception for engines with no object system (or no verified reactive cross-object mechanism).
   - **GameManager cross-engine design pattern** (this segment's central technical decision): Unity was already using a dedicated `GameManager` GameObject+script; retrofitted Scratch (new hidden `GameManager` Sprite that listens for an `[enemy hit]` broadcast and does the counting/win-check itself), Godot (new child `GameManager` Node with its own script; main scene still spawns but connects `destroyed` signal to `$GameManager.on_enemy_destroyed` instead of a local method), GameMaker (new `obj_gamemanager` object, single instance placed in the room; `obj_spawner` only spawns; `obj_enemy`'s Destroy event reaches into `obj_gamemanager` instead of `obj_spawner`), and Unreal (new `BP_GameManager` Actor Blueprint placed in the level; Level Blueprint drags in a reference to the placed instance and binds each spawned enemy's `OnEnemyDestroyed` dispatcher to `BP_GameManager`'s `HandleEnemyDestroyed` custom event instead of a Level Blueprint custom event).
   - **Documented Rule 5 exceptions** (no GameManager object introduced, with inline one-sentence rationale added to each engine's existing "Structure" bullet): GDevelop (scene variables are already global/unowned — the engine's own idiom already IS the manager pattern), TIC-80 (no object system at all — a top-level global Lua variable already is the native equivalent), 001 Game Creator (Actor Triggers are bound to the actor they're attached to, with no verified message-passing/reactive mechanism for a separate Actor to react to another Actor's destruction — avoided inventing an unverified engine feature rather than force a change I couldn't confirm was technically accurate).

For engines whose DEFAULT/main path IS the visual editor with code as the alt (Unreal, whose primary path is Blueprint) → node diagram is a TOP-LEVEL `data.level1EngineDiagram` field.

       function diagram(file, widthIn, heightIn, caption) {
         const data = fs.readFileSync(file);
         const children = [
           new Paragraph({
             alignment: AlignmentType.CENTER,
             spacing: { before: 120, after: caption ? 40 : 160 },
             children: [new ImageRun({ data, transformation: { width: widthIn * 96, height: heightIn * 96 }, type: "png" })],
           }),
         ];
         if (caption) {
           children.push(new Paragraph({
             alignment: AlignmentType.CENTER,
             spacing: { after: 160 },
             children: [new TextRun({ text: caption, italics: true, size: 16, color: "888888" })],
           }));
         }
         return children;
       }

There was a reason, but I think you're right that it's more than this level needs.

**Why it's there:** since Lesson 6, Unity's GameManager uses static members and static methods (`RegisterKill()`, `RegisterEscape()`, the shared score and lives). A static `ResetGame()` has no way to reach the enemy spawner, which is a normal scene object. So I gave the spawner a static `instance` field set in `Awake()`, and `ResetGame()` calls `EnemySpawner.instance.SpawnEnemies()`. That is the Singleton pattern. The Key even lists it as the lesson's "genuinely new C# idea".

**Other engines:** it's only in Unity. Godot has GameManager call `get_parent().spawn_enemies()`, and GameMaker uses object names directly, such as `obj_gamemanager.game_active`. Scratch uses a broadcast. In Unreal, `BP_GameManager` finds its enemies with Get All Actors of Class. Unity is the one engine where the same task needs a new design pattern. Almost certainly this is an order-of-loading problem. I haven't changed anything yet.

In the Godot design, `GameManager` is a child of the Main scene, and its `_ready()` calls `start_game()`, which calls `get_parent().spawn_enemies()`. Godot runs a child's `_ready()` before the parent has finished setting up its children. Main is still "busy" at that moment, so Main's `add_child()` is refused. The loop runs, no error shows in the game, and the enemies never enter the tree, which matches what you see.

Two checks:
1. Open the Debugger panel's Errors tab, not just the Output. You should see something like "Parent node is busy setting up children, add_child() failed. Consider using add_child.call_deferred(child) instead."
2. For a one-line fix to test, change `GameManager`'s `_ready()` from `start_game()` to `start_game.call_deferred()`. That waits until the scene has finished loading, then spawns. R-restarts shouldn't be affected, since they run later in normal play.

An alternative is to put `_ready()` back in Main's script with `$GameManager.start_game()`. That also works, because the parent's `_ready()` runs after all its children are ready. I'd go with the `call_deferred` version because it keeps the Teacher's Script line "GameManager's `_ready()` just calls `start_game()`" nearly true.

Tell me whether the error is there and whether the fix works. Then I'll update the Godot Handout and Key, and add a short note about why the deferral is needed.

human_text: what is studio mode?  I saw that referenced elsewhere but don't know what it is or how to enable it
assistant_text:
Studio Mode is an OBS feature that splits the main preview into two panes:

- **Preview (left):** where you pick and edit the next scene. Viewers can't see it.
- **Program (right):** what viewers are seeing right now.

Normally, clicking a scene puts it on stream immediately. In Studio Mode, clicking a scene only loads it into the Preview. Nothing changes for viewers until you press the **Transition** button between the two panes. That lets you check a scene and fix a source before it goes live.

To turn it on, click **Studio Mode** in the **Controls** dock, usually the lower-right panel with Start Streaming and Start Recording. If you can't find it, enable the Controls dock under **Docks** in the menu bar. Click the button again to switch it off.

For your workflow it has a trade-off. The safe pre-check is useful for a window that may not capture correctly, such as Godot's play window. But it adds a step: select the scene, then transition. Your rule is to switch scenes before every play test, so that extra step could get old fast. Also, in Studio Mode, scene hotkeys load the Preview, and you need a separate transition hotkey to take it live.

I'd try both on a normal session. If the extra step annoys you, run normal mode and use Studio Mode only when you want to check a new scene. Do you want me to soften the Studio Mode line in the notes to "optional, test it" instead of a recommendation?

You also have to tell OBS which device is your headphones: **Settings > Audio > Advanced > Monitoring Device**. Pick your headphones, not "Default". Use headphones, not speakers, or the mic will pick up its own sound and echo.

I think this is a misunderstanding about what Desktop Audio does, not a broken setup.

**What Desktop Audio is:** It copies whatever Windows plays through the default playback device into the stream. It doesn't play anything to your headphones itself, because Windows does that. So if you hear nothing in your headphones, Windows isn't sending sound to them.

**Why the mic is picking it up:** Most likely your headphones aren't the Windows default playback device, so sound comes out of a speaker (monitor or laptop speakers, say), and the mic hears it through the air. The OBS meters would then show the same sound twice, once in Desktop Audio and once in the mic.

To check, go to Windows Settings > System > Sound > Output and see which device is selected. If the headphones aren't, select them. If you want them only for some apps, use **App volume and device preferences** on the same page. Then check Desktop Audio's device in OBS under Settings > Audio. "Default" follows Windows, which is what you want.

Two related cautions:
- **Don't turn on monitoring for Desktop Audio** if Windows already plays it to your headphones. You would hear everything twice, with a delay.
- **Use either Desktop Audio or Application Audio Capture, not both.** If both capture the same app, viewers hear it twice.

You tested the beta application audio capture (the audio that goes with the window source) and it works. That is often better for this workflow, because it captures only the app you choose, so no stray notification sounds from Claude or the browser reach the stream. If you use it, I would disable Desktop Audio, or keep it only for sources you want everywhere.

assistant_text:
Multi-adapter compatibility is a Window Capture option for computers with more than one graphics adapter. That usually means a laptop with integrated graphics plus a separate GPU. It is under the **Compatibility** setting in the Window Capture properties.

If the app you're capturing is drawn by a different GPU than the one OBS is using, the capture can come back as a black or frozen image.
